prompt: Why is it important to identify individuals without symptoms that test positive for a disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They can show that it is safe to have a disease so people will not panic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are at a higher probability of dying without treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They can donate blood to sick individuals to help speed their recovery.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They can unknowingly pass the disease to others and propagate an outbreak.

answer_text: D) They can unknowingly pass the disease to others and propagate an outbreak.
explanation:
People with no symptoms who test positive can still spread the agent, but because they feel fine, they don't isolate or take precautions. They can unknowingly infect others and keep an outbreak going, so identifying them lets health officials exclude them from high-risk settings (food handling, daycare, healthcare), treat them if appropriate, and trace their contacts.

Choice A is wrong because finding asymptomatic infections is not about reassurance. Choice B is wrong because asymptomatic people are generally not at higher risk of dying. Choice C is wrong because infected people should not donate blood, and that is not a standard treatment.

Asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic transmission is why surveillance based only on symptoms misses many infections (the "iceberg" of disease), and why outbreak control may include testing contacts who have no symptoms.

prompt: What is the term used to describe the severity of a disease that an agent causes in a host?
explanation:
Virulence describes how severe the disease caused by an agent is, usually measured as the proportion of clinical cases that become severely ill or die. The question asks for the term describing severity, so the answer is virulence.

Infectivity is the ability of an agent to infect a host: the proportion of exposed people who become infected. Mortality refers to deaths in an entire population. Lethality (case fatality) is the proportion of cases who die. It is a measure of the most extreme severity and closely related to virulence, but virulence is the broader standard term for severity.

Remember the progression: infectivity (exposed to infected), pathogenicity (infected to ill), and virulence (ill to severely ill or dead). An agent can score high on one and low on another. The common cold is highly infective but has low virulence; rabies has very high virulence.

prompt: What is the term for the time between infection by a pathogen and development of symptoms?
explanation:
The incubation period is the time from exposure or infection to the onset of symptoms. During this time the agent multiplies in the host, but the person doesn't feel sick yet. Incubation periods range from hours (Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning) to days (influenza, Salmonella), weeks (hepatitis A), or even years (HIV, prions).

It is often confused with the latent period. In infectious disease, the latent period is the time from infection until the person becomes infectious; in chronic disease, latency is the time from exposure to disease onset. The period of communicability is when a person can spread the infection, and it may start before the incubation period ends.

Incubation periods are a key investigative tool. Knowing the typical range lets investigators work backward from symptom onset to estimate when exposure happened, and helps identify the likely agent.

prompt: The term used to describe the animal (usually an arthropod or insect) that indirectly transmits an infection from one host to another.
explanation:
A vector is a living organism, usually an arthropod such as a mosquito, tick, flea, louse, or fly, that carries an infectious agent from an infected host (or reservoir) to a susceptible host. Malaria and dengue (mosquitoes), Lyme disease (ticks), and plague (fleas) are classic examples. CDC classifies vector-borne spread as a form of indirect transmission.

Vectors can transmit agents mechanically (the agent rides on the vector's body or mouthparts without changing, as when flies carry bacteria on their feet) or biologically (the agent multiplies or develops inside the vector before being transmitted, as Plasmodium does inside the Anopheles mosquito).

Don't confuse a vector with a vehicle or fomite. Vehicles (food, water, blood products) and fomites (doorknobs, towels) are nonliving. Vectors are living.

prompt: The epi curve below is an example of what type of outbreak?
explanation:
This epi curve shows several successive peaks that get progressively taller, with gaps between them roughly one incubation period long. That is the classic pattern of a propagated (progressive-source) outbreak, in which the disease spreads from person to person and each wave of cases infects the next generation.

A point-source outbreak would show a single sharp peak (everyone exposed at once, as at a single meal). A continuous common-source outbreak would show a rise followed by a plateau. An intermittent common-source outbreak would show irregular peaks without the steady growth or regular spacing seen here.

This particular curve is CDC's classic example of a propagated outbreak (hepatitis A in a small community, 1970-71). Successive generations of cases with increasing size is the signature of person-to-person spread.
key_note: Successive, increasingly tall peaks roughly one incubation period apart indicate person-to-person spread.
scenario_text: Epi curve for questions 61-62.

prompt: In the epi curve from the previous question, the most likely mode of transmission is ___________________.
explanation:
A propagated epi curve means the disease is being passed from person to person: each group of cases infects the next, producing waves about one incubation period apart. The most likely mode of transmission is therefore person-to-person.

Person-to-person spread can be direct (touching, kissing, sexual contact, droplets) or indirect through fecal-oral routes and fomites, as with hepatitis A. Common-source routes such as contaminated food or water would instead produce a single peak (point source) or a plateau (continuous source).

Knowing the mode guides control. Propagated outbreaks are controlled by breaking chains of transmission: isolating cases, quarantining or giving prophylaxis to contacts, vaccination, and hygiene measures, rather than just removing a single contaminated item.
scenario_text: Epi curve for questions 61-62.

prompt: In an epi curve the horizontal x-axis denotes _____________________ while the vertical y-axis represents _______________________.
answer: Time (of onset of illness); number of cases
answer_text: Time (of onset of illness); number of cases
explanation:
An epidemic curve is a histogram of cases by time of onset of illness. The x-axis shows time (hours, days, or weeks of symptom onset), and the y-axis shows the number of cases.

The time unit on the x-axis should be chosen based on the disease's incubation period, usually somewhere between one-eighth and one-third of the average incubation period. Hours work for a short-incubation toxin outbreak; days or weeks work for diseases like hepatitis A. Too broad an interval hides the pattern, and too narrow an interval makes the curve choppy.

From an epi curve you can read the magnitude of the outbreak, its time trend, likely outbreak type (point, continuous, intermittent, or propagated), outliers, and an estimated exposure period by working backward from onset using the incubation period.

prompt: In an epi curve, an outlier can be defined as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cases that are failed to be diagnosed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cases that are linked directly to the index case.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cases that occur at the beginning or end of the outbreak.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cases that stand apart from the overall pattern.

answer_text: D) Cases that stand apart from the overall pattern.
explanation:
An outlier on an epi curve is a case that stands apart from the overall pattern, for example a case occurring well before or well after the main cluster. Outliers are worth investigating because they can reveal useful information: an early case might be the source (such as an infected food handler), a late case might represent secondary person-to-person spread, and an unrelated case might be background illness that doesn't fit the case definition.

Choice A describes undiagnosed cases, which wouldn't appear on the curve at all. Choice B describes secondary or linked cases. Choice C is only partly right: outliers often occur at the beginning or end, but the defining feature is that they don't fit the pattern, not just when they happened.

CDC's classic example: in a point-source outbreak, a case several days before the peak may be the person who contaminated the food.

prompt: Which of the following is information that an epi curve can provide?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The severity of symptoms in affected individuals

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distribution of cases over time

choices.label: E
choices.text: The presence or absence of outliers

answer_text: A) The magnitude of an outbreak; C) The distribution of cases over time; E) The presence or absence of outliers
explanation:
An epi curve shows the number of cases by time of onset, so it can show the magnitude of the outbreak (how many cases and how high the peak), the time distribution (when it started, peaked, and ended, and the overall trend), and outliers (cases that don't fit the pattern). It can also suggest the type of outbreak and the likely exposure period.

An epi curve can't show how severe symptoms were (B), since it counts cases rather than measuring severity, and it can't by itself prove the cause of the outbreak (D). The shape gives clues about the mode of spread, but identifying the actual source requires analytic studies and lab testing. Because B and D are wrong, "All of the above" (F) is also wrong.

Epi curves are part of descriptive epidemiology (the "time" in person, place, and time). They generate hypotheses that are then tested with analytic epidemiology.

prompt: Relative risk and odds ratios are both important measures for determining the strength of association.
explanation:
Relative risk (RR) and the odds ratio (OR) are both measures of association: they quantify how strongly an exposure is linked with an outcome. Values further from 1 indicate stronger associations, and Bradford Hill's first criterion, strength of association, is usually judged with these measures. The statement is true.

RR compares the risk of disease in exposed and unexposed people and is used in cohort studies and outbreak investigations of defined groups. OR compares the odds of exposure in cases and controls and is used in case-control studies. When disease is rare, the OR approximates the RR.

Other measures of association include the attributable risk (the risk difference) and the prevalence ratio from cross-sectional studies. A strong association alone doesn't prove causation, but it is one piece of evidence.

prompt: Attributable risk determines the amount a person is at fault for when they contract a disease and takes into account genetic, social, and external factors.
explanation:
Attributable risk (also called the risk difference) is the risk of disease in the exposed group minus the risk in the unexposed group. It measures how much of the disease risk among exposed people can be attributed to the exposure. It has nothing to do with personal blame or fault, and it isn't a combination of genetic and social factors. The statement is false.

For example, if 20% of smokers and 2% of non-smokers develop a disease, the attributable risk is 18 percentage points. The attributable risk percent (AR% = (Re − Ru)/Re) tells you what share of disease in the exposed would be prevented by removing the exposure, here 90%.

There is also the population attributable risk, which considers how common the exposure is in the whole population, and is useful for setting public health priorities.
key_note: Attributable risk is the risk difference (risk in exposed minus risk in unexposed): the excess risk due to the exposure.

prompt: An endemic disease spikes suddenly before achieving a steady state across the world.
explanation:
An endemic disease is one that is constantly present at its usual, expected level in a population or geographic area. It does not spike suddenly, and it doesn't refer to the whole world. The statement mixes up several terms and is false.

A sudden increase above the expected level is an epidemic (or an outbreak, if localized). An epidemic spreading across several countries or continents is a pandemic. A disease can become endemic after an epidemic phase, as some argue COVID-19 did, but endemic itself describes the stable baseline, not the spike.

Endemic levels can be low (hypoendemic), high (hyperendemic), or near-universal (holoendemic).

prompt: The difference between an endemic and pandemic disease is the geographic distribution it affects.
explanation:
The difference between endemic and pandemic isn't only geographic. Endemic describes the usual, baseline level of a disease in an area: it is about level relative to what is expected. A pandemic is an epidemic (cases above what is expected) that spreads over several countries or continents, usually affecting many people. So the two terms differ in level relative to expected occurrence as well as in spread. The key marks the statement false, which fits that reasoning.

You can have a widespread endemic disease (malaria across much of the tropics) that is not a pandemic, because it is occurring at its usual level. A pandemic, like influenza in 1918 or 2009 or COVID-19 in 2020, involves an increase above the expected level across a large area.

This one is debatable, since geography is part of the difference. On a test, the safest reasoning is that endemic is about the expected level of disease, while pandemic adds both an above-expected increase and global spread.
key_note: Endemic means the constant baseline level in an area. A pandemic is an epidemic (above-expected level) spreading over several countries or continents. They differ in both level relative to expected and in spread, not geography alone.

prompt: Which of the following terms best describes the COVID-19 outbreak in 2020-2021?
explanation:
In 2020 and 2021, COVID-19 spread rapidly to nearly every country in the world, causing case numbers far above any expected level. That is a pandemic: an epidemic occurring over a very wide area, crossing international boundaries, and usually affecting many people. The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic on March 11, 2020.

Endemic describes a stable baseline level, which it was not during 2020-21. Epidemic is technically true but less specific: a pandemic is a global epidemic, and the question asks for the best term. "Steady state" is not an epidemiologic classification.

Other pandemics include the 1918 influenza pandemic, the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, and HIV/AIDS.

prompt: Which of the following terms best describes COVID-19 today?
explanation:
COVID-19 is now generally considered endemic: it continues to circulate with fairly predictable patterns (including seasonal waves) and is managed as an ongoing respiratory disease rather than an emergency. The WHO ended the COVID-19 public health emergency of international concern in May 2023.

It is no longer best described as a pandemic, because most people have some immunity and it no longer causes the explosive, above-expected spread of 2020-21. "Epidemic" would imply cases far above the expected level. "Steady state" is not a standard term.

Endemic doesn't mean harmless or constant. Endemic diseases can still cause many deaths and seasonal peaks (seasonal influenza is endemic), and they can produce new epidemics when a new variant appears or immunity wanes.

prompt: Calculate the risk of developing measles in the unvaccinated group.
explanation:
The risk (incidence proportion, or attack rate) is the number of new cases divided by the population at risk. Among unvaccinated students, 36 developed measles out of 120 unvaccinated students. Risk = 36/120 = 0.30, or 30%.

The denominator is the total number of unvaccinated students (36 + 84 = 120), not just those who stayed well (84). Using 84 would give the odds (36/84 = 0.43), a different quantity used in odds ratios.

A 30% attack rate is very high, which is typical of measles, one of the most contagious diseases known. In unvaccinated, close-contact settings like schools, a single case can infect most susceptible people around them.
scenario_text:
There is a measles outbreak at a local high school. The local health department is deployed to evaluate the situation and create the table below.

| | Measles | No Measles | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unvaccinated | 36 | 84 | 120 |
| Vaccinated | 12 | 268 | 280 |
| Total | 48 | 352 | 400 |

prompt: Calculate the risk of developing measles in the vaccinated group.
explanation:
Among vaccinated students, 12 developed measles out of 280 vaccinated students. Risk = 12/280 = 0.043, or about 4.3%.

Even with a vaccine, some vaccinated people get sick, because no vaccine is 100% effective (two doses of MMR are about 97% effective against measles). In a large group of vaccinated people, a small number of breakthrough cases is expected.

These two risks (30% in the unvaccinated and 4.3% in the vaccinated) are the inputs for the relative risk and for vaccine effectiveness: VE = (30% − 4.3%)/30% ≈ 86% in this outbreak.

explanation:
Relative risk = risk in the unvaccinated ÷ risk in the vaccinated = (36/120)/(12/280) = 0.300/0.04286 = 7.0. The original key gave 6.98 because it rounded 12/280 to 0.043 before dividing. Using unrounded values gives exactly 7.0, and either answer should earn credit.

An RR of 7 means unvaccinated students were seven times as likely to get measles as vaccinated students, a very strong association. Here the "exposure" being studied is lack of vaccination.

General rule: avoid rounding intermediate values in multi-step calculations. Keep full precision until the final answer, then round as instructed.

prompt: Based on your calculation the ________________ group is _____________ times more likely to contract measles than the ____________________ group.
explanation:
The relative risk compares the unvaccinated group with the vaccinated group, so the sentence reads: "the unvaccinated group is 7 times more likely to contract measles than the vaccinated group."

Get the order right. RR = (risk in the group in the numerator)/(risk in the group in the denominator). Because the unvaccinated risk is on top, the unvaccinated group is the one that is 7 times as likely. Flipping it would give the vaccinated group an RR of 1/7 ≈ 0.14, a protective effect.

Strictly, "7 times as likely" is more accurate than "7 times more likely" (which could mean 8 times as likely), but most tests treat the two phrases the same.

prompt: Calculate the odds ratio for this outbreak.
explanation:
The odds ratio compares the odds of disease in each group. Odds in the unvaccinated = 36/84 = 0.4286. Odds in the vaccinated = 12/268 = 0.0448. OR = 0.4286/0.0448 = 9.57. Using the cross-product formula: OR = (a × d)/(b × c) = (36 × 268)/(84 × 12) = 9648/1008 = 9.57.

The OR (9.57) is larger than the RR (7.0). This always happens when the disease is common: here 30% of the unvaccinated got measles, so the "rare disease" assumption that makes OR ≈ RR doesn't hold. The OR exaggerates the strength of association compared with the RR when the outcome is common.

Because this is an outbreak in a defined population (the school), where you know everyone at risk, the relative risk is the more appropriate measure. The OR is mainly used in case-control studies.

prompt: Calculate the crude overall relative risk of Legionnaires' Disease for those with Chronic Lung Disease vs those without. How many times more likely are individuals with Chronic Lung Disease (CLD) vs those without to develop the disease?
answer: Risk with CLD = 88/250 = 0.352; risk without = 34/650 = 0.0523; RR = 6.73 (about 7 times as likely)
answer_text: Risk with CLD = 88/250 = 0.352; risk without = 34/650 = 0.0523; RR = 6.73 (about 7 times as likely)
explanation:
Crude RR for chronic lung disease (CLD): risk with CLD = 88/250 = 0.352; risk without CLD = 34/650 = 0.0523; RR = 0.352/0.0523 = 6.73. People with chronic lung disease were about 7 times as likely to develop Legionnaires' disease.

The original key gave 6.77, which comes from rounding 34/650 to 0.052 before dividing. The unrounded answer is 6.73, and "about 7 times" is fine for the interpretation.

"Crude" means the RR is calculated from the combined data without accounting for other variables. The next questions stratify by pool exposure to see whether the CLD–Legionnaires' association differs depending on pool use, which is how you check for confounding or effect modification.
key_note: 6.77 comes from rounding 34/650 to 0.052; the unrounded value is 6.73.

| No Chronic Lung Disease | 34 | 616 | 650 |

| CLD Status | Legionnaires + | Legionnaires - | Total |

prompt: What is the relative risk of contracting the disease if they visited the pool based on having or not having CLD?
explanation:
Among people exposed to the pool (Table 2): risk with CLD = 50/100 = 0.50; risk without CLD = 20/200 = 0.10; RR = 0.50/0.10 = 5.0. Among pool users, people with chronic lung disease were 5 times as likely to develop Legionnaires' disease as those without.

This is a stratum-specific RR: the association between CLD and disease within one level (pool exposure) of a third variable. Comparing it with the RR in the other stratum (no pool, Q80) and with the crude RR (Q77) tells you how pool exposure relates to the CLD association.

Pool users had high risk regardless of lung disease (10% even without CLD), which fits what is known about Legionella: it grows in warm water systems and spreads through aerosolized water.

prompt: What is the relative risk if they did not visit the pool based on having or not having CLD?
explanation:
Among people not exposed to the pool (Table 3): risk with CLD = 38/150 = 0.253; risk without CLD = 14/450 = 0.0311; RR = 0.253/0.0311 = 8.14. The original key gave 8.16 because of rounding.

In this stratum, CLD carries an 8-fold increase in risk, compared with a 5-fold increase among pool users and a crude RR of about 6.7. The stratum-specific RRs differ noticeably from each other.

When the two stratum RRs are similar to each other but different from the crude RR, the third variable is a confounder. When the stratum RRs differ meaningfully from each other, the third variable is an effect modifier. Here 5.0 and 8.1 differ, which points to effect modification (Q81).

prompt: In this case the aquatic center is considered to be what?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A separate source of an outbreak

explanation:
Effect modification occurs when the association between an exposure and an outcome differs across levels of a third variable. Here, the RR for chronic lung disease is 5.0 among pool users and 8.1 among non-users. The effect of CLD on Legionnaires' risk depends on pool exposure, so the pool (aquatic center) is an effect modifier.

A confounder would make the crude RR misleading, but the stratum-specific RRs would be similar to each other. In confounding, the crude RR typically falls outside the range of the stratum RRs. Here the crude RR (6.7) lies between the two stratum values, the classic sign of effect modification. The pool may also be a separate source of Legionella exposure, but that doesn't describe its statistical role in this analysis. "All of the above" and "None of the above" are therefore wrong.

Effect modification is a real biological or social difference that should be reported separately for each stratum. Confounding is a distortion that should be adjusted away.
key_note: The stratum-specific RRs (5.0 with pool, 8.1 without) differ from each other, and the crude RR (6.7) lies between them. That pattern is effect modification, not confounding.

prompt: Clinical (C) or public health (P)? A surgeon notices a nosocomial infection spreading through the improper sanitation of a particular tool and updates sanitation requirements in his practice only.
explanation:
The key calls this clinical. The surgeon changes sanitation requirements only in his own practice, in response to infections among his patients.

It's debatable. Changing infection-control procedures protects a group of patients, which has a public health flavor. But because the change is limited to one practice and doesn't involve population-level surveillance or policy, it falls on the clinical side.

Hospital infection control often blends the two approaches.
key_note: Debatable: changing infection-control procedures protects a group of patients, but it is limited to his own clinical practice.

prompt: Clinical (C) or public health (P)? A patient has chickenpox, so the whole family gets vaccinated by the nurse as post-exposure management.
explanation:
Clinical. A nurse vaccinating one patient's family members after exposure is individual-level care for specific people.

Post-exposure vaccination for chickenpox works if given within 3–5 days of exposure.

Public health would get involved if the case were part of a larger outbreak, for example in a school.

prompt: Clinical (C) or public health (P)? A doctor reports an uptick in cholera in a particular neighborhood to the CDC, which then closes a particular water pump in the area.
explanation:

This mirrors John Snow's removal of the Broad Street pump handle in 1854.

Reporting by clinicians feeds public health action.

prompt: Who created the polio vaccine and who developed the oral version of this vaccine?
answer: Jonas Salk - inactivated (injected) polio vaccine; Albert Sabin - oral (live attenuated) polio vaccine
answer_text: Jonas Salk - inactivated (injected) polio vaccine; Albert Sabin - oral (live attenuated) polio vaccine
explanation:
Jonas Salk developed the inactivated (injected) polio vaccine, licensed in 1955. Albert Sabin developed the oral, live-attenuated polio vaccine, licensed in the early 1960s.

The oral vaccine was cheaper, easier to give, and produced intestinal immunity, which made it central to global eradication efforts.

The live oral vaccine can rarely mutate and cause vaccine-derived polio, so the U.S. now uses only the inactivated vaccine.

prompt: John Snow's research refuted the then-current Miasma theory. Explain the Miasma theory and how John Snow refuted it.
answer: Miasma theory held that diseases such as cholera were caused by 'bad air' - noxious vapors from rotting organic matter. Snow mapped cholera deaths clustering around the Broad Street pump (deaths fell after the handle was removed). He also compared death rates in households supplied by the Southwark & Vauxhall company (sewage-contaminated Thames water) and the Lambeth company (cleaner water), showing cholera was spread by contaminated water, not air.

explanation:
Miasma theory held that diseases such as cholera were caused by "bad air," noxious vapors from rotting organic matter.

Snow mapped cholera deaths and found they clustered around the Broad Street pump. Deaths fell after the pump handle was removed. He also compared death rates in households supplied by the Southwark & Vauxhall company (sewage-contaminated Thames water) and the Lambeth company (cleaner water). This showed cholera spread through contaminated water, not air.

His work came before germ theory was accepted. Koch identified Vibrio cholerae in 1883.

prompt: Define analytical epidemiology and explain how John Snow incorporated it into his study.
answer: Analytical epidemiology compares groups to test hypotheses about the causes (how and why) of disease. Snow compared cholera death rates between households served by two water companies (a 'natural experiment'), showing far higher mortality among those drinking Southwark & Vauxhall water.
answer_text: Analytical epidemiology compares groups to test hypotheses about the causes (how and why) of disease. Snow compared cholera death rates between households served by two water companies (a 'natural experiment'), showing far higher mortality among those drinking Southwark & Vauxhall water.
explanation:
Analytical epidemiology compares groups to test hypotheses about the causes of disease, the how and why.

Snow compared cholera death rates between households served by two water companies, a "natural experiment." Mortality was far higher among households drinking Southwark & Vauxhall water.

Because the companies' customers were mixed together in the same neighborhoods, the comparison controlled for many confounders.

answer_text: a. Clinical disease (early nonspecific symptoms); b. Subclinical disease; c. Recovery, disability or death; d. Subclinical disease
explanation:
a. Prodromal period: clinical disease (early, nonspecific symptoms). b. Incubation period: subclinical disease. c. Convalescent period: recovery, disability, or death. d. Prepatent period: subclinical disease.

She treated the wound as usual. A few days later she got a mild fever and dysphagia. She went to the doctor and found out she has tetanus.

prompt: Identify all 6 parts of the chain of infection and apply them to Florene's disease.
answer: Infectious agent: Clostridium tetani (spores / tetanospasmin toxin). Reservoir: soil, dust and animal intestines/feces at the park. Portal of exit: animal feces into the soil. Mode of transmission: indirect - spores in soil or on the concrete contaminating the wound. Portal of entry: the open wound (broken skin). Susceptible host: Florene (likely not up to date on tetanus boosters).
answer_text: Infectious agent: Clostridium tetani (spores / tetanospasmin toxin). Reservoir: soil, dust and animal intestines/feces at the park. Portal of exit: animal feces into the soil. Susceptible host: Florene (likely not up to date on tetanus boosters).
explanation:
The chain of infection for Florene's tetanus: - **Infectious agent:** Clostridium tetani (spores and the toxin tetanospasmin). - **Reservoir:** soil, dust, and animal intestines and feces at the park. - **Portal of exit:** animal feces into the soil. - **Mode of transmission:** indirect, through spores in the soil or on the concrete contaminating the wound. - **Portal of entry:** the open wound (broken skin). - **Susceptible host:** Florene, who was likely not up to date on tetanus boosters.

Tetanus isn't spread from person to person.

Prevention: keep up tetanus boosters (every 10 years), and give a booster after a dirty wound if the last dose was more than 5 years ago.

prompt: Which study design is most prone to both recall bias and selection bias?
explanation:
Case-control studies are the most prone to both recall bias and selection bias. They rely on participants remembering past exposures, and controls must be chosen carefully so they represent the source population.

Prospective cohorts (A) and RCTs (C) collect exposure data before outcomes occur, which limits recall bias. Ecological studies (D) are mainly prone to the ecological fallacy.

Careful control selection and objective exposure records reduce these biases.

prompt: You want to study the long-term cardiovascular effects of a drug that patients took 10 years ago. Which study design is most appropriate?
explanation:
A retrospective cohort fits best. You use existing records to identify who took the drug 10 years ago (exposed) and who didn't, then compare their cardiovascular outcomes since then.

A prospective cohort (A) would mean waiting 10 more years. A case-control study (C) starts from outcomes. A cross-sectional study (D) can't establish temporality.

Retrospective cohorts are efficient when good historical records exist.

prompt: From a cohort of 10,000 people followed for 10 years, a researcher selects all people who develop stroke and a random sample of those who do not for detailed exposure assessment. What study design is this?
explanation:
Selecting all people who develop stroke (cases) and a random sample of those who don't (controls), both from within an existing cohort, is a nested case-control study.

In a case-cohort design, the comparison subcohort is sampled from the whole cohort regardless of outcome. Here the controls are sampled from non-cases, which makes it nested case-control.

This design is efficient when detailed exposure assessment is expensive, such as biomarker testing on stored samples.
key_note: In a case-cohort design the comparison subcohort is sampled from the whole cohort regardless of outcome. Here controls are sampled from non-cases, which makes it a nested case-control study.

prompt: Which of the following is not a type of selection bias?
explanation:
Observer bias isn't a type of selection bias. It's an information (measurement) bias.

Berkson's bias (A), Neyman bias (B), and the healthy worker effect (C) are all selection biases.

Selection bias comes from how participants are chosen. Information bias comes from how data are measured.
key_note: Observer bias is an information (measurement) bias.

Tetrodotoxin (A) comes from pufferfish. Staphylococcal enterotoxin (C) causes vomiting. C. perfringens toxin (D) causes diarrhea.

Botulism causes descending flaccid paralysis and needs antitoxin and often mechanical ventilation.

prompt: Which technique would be least useful for differentiating very closely related bacterial isolates in a hospital outbreak?
explanation:
Serotyping is the least useful for telling apart very closely related isolates. It classifies bacteria only by surface antigens, which many unrelated strains share.

PFGE, WGS, and SNP analysis give much finer resolution.

Serotyping is useful for broad classification, for example Salmonella serotypes, but not for outbreak-level discrimination.

prompt: PFGE cannot detect which of the following?
explanation:
PFGE can't detect point mutations (SNPs), unless the mutation happens to create or destroy a restriction site.

PFGE does detect large rearrangements, insertions, and differences in restriction fragment patterns.

That's why WGS replaced PFGE for high-resolution outbreak detection.

Investigators would look for several contaminated products or suppliers.

answer_text: Vaccination primes antibodies against pertussis toxin and other antigens and creates memory responses, so the immune system neutralizes the toxin and controls the infection faster, limiting airway damage and severity.
explanation:
Vaccination primes antibodies against pertussis toxin and other antigens and creates immune memory. The immune system can then neutralize the toxin and control the infection faster, which limits airway damage and severity.

Vaccinated people who get sick often have milder, shorter illness without the classic whoop.

Milder disease in vaccinated people can also make diagnosis and surveillance harder.

Penicillin was mass-produced in the 1940s by Florey and Chain and transformed the treatment of bacterial infections.

Fleming also warned early on about antibiotic resistance.

prompt: What is the difference between descriptive epidemiology and analytical epidemiology?
answer: Descriptive epidemiology describes disease by person, place and time (who, what, when, where) and generates hypotheses. Analytic epidemiology tests hypotheses by comparing groups to identify associations between exposures and outcomes (how and why).
answer_text: Descriptive epidemiology describes disease by person, place and time (who, what, when, where) and generates hypotheses. Analytic epidemiology tests hypotheses by comparing groups to identify associations between exposures and outcomes (how and why).
explanation:
Descriptive epidemiology describes disease by person, place, and time: who is affected, where, and when. It answers "who, what, when, and where" and generates hypotheses.

Analytic epidemiology tests those hypotheses. It compares groups, such as exposed vs. unexposed or cases vs. controls, to find associations between exposures and outcomes. It answers "how and why," using cohort, case-control, and experimental studies.

In an outbreak investigation, descriptive work (line lists, epi curves, spot maps) comes first and suggests a likely source. Analytic studies then test it with relative risks or odds ratios.

prompt: What is the difference between the clinical approach and the public health approach to health care?
answer: The clinical approach focuses on diagnosing and treating illness in individual patients; the public health approach focuses on controlling and preventing disease in populations or groups.
answer_text: The clinical approach focuses on diagnosing and treating illness in individual patients; the public health approach focuses on controlling and preventing disease in populations or groups.
explanation:
The clinical approach diagnoses and treats illness in individual patients. The public health approach focuses on controlling and preventing disease in populations or groups.

A clinician asks, "What's wrong with this patient, and how do I treat them?" A public health practitioner asks, "What's affecting this community, why, and how do we prevent it?"

The two work together. Clinicians report cases to public health surveillance, and public health findings guide clinical practice, such as screening and vaccination recommendations.

prompt: What is the difference between the incubation and latency period?
answer: Both occur during the subclinical stage. Incubation period: time from exposure to an infectious agent until onset of symptoms. Latent period (per key): time from exposure until the person becomes infectious. In chronic disease epidemiology, 'latency' also means the time from exposure to disease onset.
answer_text: Both occur during the subclinical stage. Incubation period: time from exposure to an infectious agent until onset of symptoms. Latent period (per key): time from exposure until the person becomes infectious. In chronic disease epidemiology, 'latency' also means the time from exposure to disease onset.
explanation:
Both periods happen during the subclinical stage of disease. The incubation period runs from exposure to an infectious agent until symptoms begin. The latent period, as the key defines it, runs from exposure until the person becomes infectious.

The difference matters for disease control. If the latent period is shorter than the incubation period, people can transmit before they have symptoms, which makes control harder. COVID-19 is an example.

In chronic disease epidemiology, "latency" means something different: the time from exposure to disease onset. Asbestos and mesothelioma, decades apart, is an example. The two meanings come up in different contexts.

prompt: Most known for his work in tracing the source of a cholera outbreak in London and as "the father of epidemiology", he worked as a surgeon and general practitioner as part of the Westminster Medical Society.
explanation:
John Snow traced the source of the 1854 London cholera outbreak to the Broad Street pump and is called the "father of epidemiology." He was a surgeon and general practitioner and an active member of the Westminster Medical Society.

He also pioneered anesthesia, giving chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth.

His mapping of cases and his "Grand Experiment," comparing water companies, are the foundations of field epidemiology.

prompt: A new disease emerges, and its reproduction number (R0) is estimated to be 6. This means that:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The disease will cause 6 deaths for every 100 people infected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every infected person will infect 6 others on average.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 people will be infected out of 100 people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 6 percent of the population is affected with this disease.

answer_text: B) Every infected person will infect 6 others on average.
explanation:
R0 (the basic reproduction number) is the average number of secondary infections caused by one infected person in a fully susceptible population. An R0 of 6 means each infected person infects about 6 others on average.

R0 isn't a mortality rate (A), an attack rate (C), or a prevalence (D).

When R0 is greater than 1, a disease can spread. When it's less than 1, it dies out. Higher R0 means higher vaccination coverage is needed for herd immunity.
key_note: Strictly, 6 others on average in a fully susceptible population.

prompt: Calculate the herd immunity threshold (HIT) of this disease (R0 = 6) assuming vaccine efficacy is 100%. Show your work, round to the nearest hundredth.
explanation:
The herd immunity threshold is HIT = 1 − 1/R0 = 1 − 1/6 = 0.8333, or 83.33%.

At least 83.33% of the population must be immune to stop sustained transmission.

With 100% vaccine efficacy, the required vaccination coverage equals the HIT.

prompt: What if the vaccine efficacy is less than 100%? What happens to the herd immunity threshold as the vaccine efficacy decreases? Explain why.
answer: The vaccination coverage needed (HIT/VE) increases as efficacy decreases, because fewer vaccinated people are actually immune, so a larger share of the population must be vaccinated. If efficacy is low enough, required coverage exceeds 100% and herd immunity cannot be reached by vaccination alone.
answer_text: The vaccination coverage needed (HIT/VE) increases as efficacy decreases, because fewer vaccinated people are actually immune, so a larger share of the population must be vaccinated. If efficacy is low enough, required coverage exceeds 100% and herd immunity cannot be reached by vaccination alone.
explanation:
The HIT itself (1 − 1/R0) depends only on R0, so it stays the same. What changes is the vaccination coverage needed to reach it: required coverage = HIT ÷ VE. As vaccine efficacy decreases, coverage must increase, because fewer vaccinated people actually become immune.

For example, with VE = 90%, coverage must be 83.33% ÷ 0.90 ≈ 92.6%. If VE is low enough, required coverage goes above 100%, and herd immunity can't be reached by vaccination alone.

This explains why measles needs about 95% coverage. Its R0 is high and the vaccine, though very effective, isn't perfect.
key_note: Strictly, the HIT itself (1 − 1/R0) is unchanged; it is the vaccination coverage needed to reach it that rises.

prompt: In a study examining the relationship between smoking and lung cancer, the researchers failed to account for exposure to air pollution, which is a known risk factor for lung cancer. This introduces:
explanation:
Failing to account for air pollution, a known risk factor for lung cancer that may also be associated with smoking, introduces confounding (confounder bias). The smoking–lung cancer association might be partly due to air pollution.

Observer bias (A), instrument bias (B), and information bias (D) are measurement errors, not third-variable effects.

Confounding can be controlled by measuring the confounder and adjusting for it through stratification or regression.

prompt: A study on the link between respiratory disease and bone disease only uses hospitalized patients. This might lead to a false association because people with both conditions are more likely to be hospitalized than those with just one, which is called:
explanation:
Berkson's bias is a form of selection bias found in hospital-based studies. People with two conditions are more likely to be hospitalized than people with only one, which creates a false association between the conditions.

Berkson's bias is a specific type of selection bias, so C is partially correct, but D is the most precise answer. Surveillance bias (A) comes from more intensive testing in some groups. Confounder bias (B) is a third-variable effect.

Using community-based samples instead of only hospitalized patients helps avoid Berkson's bias.
key_note: Berkson's bias is a specific type of selection bias, so C is partially correct.

prompt: If a study compares the mortality of factory workers to the general public, the workers may appear healthier simply because they are fit enough to hold a job. This is called:
explanation:
The healthy worker effect is a type of selection bias. Employed people tend to be healthier than the general population, which includes people too ill to work, so workers appear to have lower mortality.

This can hide real occupational hazards when workers are compared with the general public.

A better approach is to compare workers with other workers, for example exposed vs. unexposed employees.

prompt: In a study testing a new drug for chronic pain over several months, patients whose pain isn't improving or those who experience side effects may drop out, while those feeling better stay. This can cause the results to overestimate the drug's effectiveness. This introduces:
explanation:
Attrition bias happens when participants drop out unevenly. Patients who aren't improving or who have side effects leave the study, while those who feel better stay, so the drug looks more effective than it is.

Recall bias (B) involves memory. Instrument bias (C) involves measurement tools. Confounder bias (D) involves a third variable.

Intention-to-treat analysis and minimizing loss to follow-up help reduce attrition bias.

prompt: In a study examining the relationship between smoking and lung cancer, an interviewer might ask more probing questions about smoking habits to a participant they know has lung cancer than to a healthy control. This introduces:
explanation:
Observer (interviewer) bias occurs when an investigator's knowledge of a participant's disease status affects how they collect data, such as asking more probing questions of cases.

Observer bias is a type of information bias, so C is also technically correct. A is the more specific answer. Berkson's bias (B) is selection bias in hospital studies, and instrument bias (D) comes from faulty measurement tools.

Blinding interviewers to case status and using standardized questionnaires reduce observer bias.
key_note: Observer (interviewer) bias is a type of information bias.

prompt: A study looks at city-level data to compare average sugar consumption and obesity rates across 50 cities. Individual-level data is not collected.
explanation:
Comparing city-level averages of sugar consumption and obesity rates, with no individual-level data, is an ecologic study.

Ecologic studies use groups, such as cities or countries, as the unit of analysis.

They're cheap and useful for generating hypotheses, but they're prone to the ecological fallacy: assuming that group-level associations apply to individuals.

explanation:
Influenza spreading after a student sneezed without covering their mouth is droplet transmission. Large respiratory droplets travel short distances, usually less than about 6 feet, and land on mucous membranes.

Droplet spread is a form of direct transmission. It differs from airborne spread, which involves small particles that stay suspended over longer distances.

Covering coughs and sneezes, masks, and distancing reduce droplet transmission.

prompt: A vaccination program is provided to all children to prevent measles.
explanation:
Vaccinating all children to prevent measles is primary prevention. It prevents disease in healthy people before exposure or infection.

Primordial prevention (A) addresses root social and environmental conditions. Secondary (C) detects disease early. Tertiary (D) limits complications of established disease. Quaternary (E) avoids overmedicalization.

Vaccination is the classic example of primary prevention.

prompt: Urban planners redesign neighborhoods with bike lanes and parks to reduce future cardiovascular disease risk in the population.
explanation:
Redesigning neighborhoods with bike lanes and parks to reduce future cardiovascular risk is primordial prevention. It changes environmental and social conditions so risk factors such as physical inactivity don't develop in the first place.

It's population-wide and comes before individual risk factors, which makes it primordial rather than primary.

Other examples include tobacco control laws and sugar taxes.

prompt: Patients who have had a stroke attend rehabilitation to regain mobility and prevent future complications.
explanation:
Stroke rehabilitation to regain mobility and prevent complications is tertiary prevention. It reduces disability and complications from established disease.

Tertiary prevention includes rehabilitation, chronic disease management, and support groups.

It aims to improve quality of life and function.

prompt: Individuals with prediabetes attend a lifestyle modification program to prevent progression to type 2 diabetes.
explanation:
The key says secondary prevention, on the view that prediabetes is an early stage of disease, and the program stops it from progressing.

However, prediabetes is usually considered a risk state, not diabetes itself. Programs like the CDC's Diabetes Prevention Program are generally called primary prevention of type 2 diabetes. Primary (B) is arguably the better answer.

These levels can overlap depending on how the condition is defined. Explaining your reasoning matters on free-response versions of this question.
key_note: Prediabetes is a risk state, not diabetes. Programs like the CDC Diabetes Prevention Program are generally called primary prevention of type 2 diabetes. The key's 'secondary' treats prediabetes as early-stage disease.

explanation:
Reducing unnecessary imaging tests in low-risk patients to prevent radiation exposure is quaternary prevention: protecting patients from harm caused by excessive medical intervention.

Quaternary prevention addresses overdiagnosis, overtreatment, and iatrogenic harm.

The Choosing Wisely campaign promotes quaternary prevention by identifying unnecessary tests and treatments.

prompt: A clinic screens adults for high blood pressure during annual check-ups to detect hypertension early.
explanation:
Screening adults for high blood pressure during annual checkups is secondary prevention. It detects disease early, before symptoms or complications, so treatment can start.

Hypertension is often called the "silent killer" because it usually has no symptoms. Screening allows early treatment, which prevents stroke, heart attack, and kidney disease.

Other examples include mammograms, Pap smears, and colonoscopies.

prompt: Cancer survivors participate in physical therapy and counseling to improve quality of life and reduce long-term complications.
explanation:
Cancer survivors doing physical therapy and counseling to improve quality of life and reduce long-term complications is tertiary prevention. It limits disability and complications from disease that has already occurred.

Tertiary prevention includes rehabilitation, survivorship care, and managing chronic disease.

Primordial and primary prevention act before disease, secondary prevention detects it early, and quaternary prevention avoids overtreatment.

prompt: A doctor decides not to prescribe antibiotics for a patient with a viral infection to avoid unnecessary harm.
explanation:
A doctor not prescribing antibiotics for a viral infection is quaternary prevention. It protects the patient from unnecessary treatment and the harm that can follow, such as side effects, C. difficile infection, and antibiotic resistance.

Antibiotics don't work against viruses, so prescribing them brings risk with no benefit.

Antibiotic stewardship also has population-level benefits, because it slows the development of antimicrobial resistance.

These policies act at the population level, before individual risk factors appear. They aren't primary prevention, which targets people at risk for a specific disease.

Many primordial strategies are policies, laws, or urban design.

On December 6th, several students at Chaboya Middle School visited the nurse complaining of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps. A few students also reported low grade fever. Over the next two days absenteeism increased among the seventh-graders.

prompt: What are Koch's postulates?
answer: 1) The microorganism must be found in abundance in all organisms with the disease, but not in healthy organisms. 2) It must be isolated from a diseased organism and grown in pure culture. 3) The cultured microorganism should cause disease when introduced into a healthy, susceptible host. 4) It must be re-isolated from the experimentally infected host and identified as identical to the original agent.
answer_text: 1) The microorganism must be found in abundance in all organisms with the disease, but not in healthy organisms. 2) It must be isolated from a diseased organism and grown in pure culture. 3) The cultured microorganism should cause disease when introduced into a healthy, susceptible host. 4) It must be re-isolated from the experimentally infected host and identified as identical to the original agent.
explanation:
Koch's postulates are criteria for showing that a specific microorganism causes a specific disease. First, the microorganism must be found in abundance in all organisms with the disease, but not in healthy ones. Second, it must be isolated and grown in pure culture. Third, the cultured microorganism must cause the same disease when introduced into a healthy, susceptible host. Fourth, it must be re-isolated from that host and identified as identical to the original.

Robert Koch developed these in the 1880s, working on anthrax and tuberculosis.

They provided a rigorous framework for germ theory and microbial causation.

prompt: What are 2 limitations of Koch's postulates?
answer: Any two: asymptomatic carriers violate postulate 1; many agents cannot be grown in pure culture (viruses, prions, M. leprae); one pathogen can cause several diseases and some diseases need multiple factors; ethically you cannot infect humans; they do not apply to noninfectious/chronic diseases.
answer_text: Any two: asymptomatic carriers violate postulate 1; many agents cannot be grown in pure culture (viruses, prions, M. leprae); one pathogen can cause several diseases and some diseases need multiple factors; ethically you cannot infect humans; they do not apply to noninfectious/chronic diseases.
explanation:
Limitations of Koch's postulates include asymptomatic carriers, which violate the first postulate, and organisms that cannot be grown in pure culture, such as viruses, prions, and Mycobacterium leprae.

Other limitations: one pathogen can cause multiple diseases, and some diseases need multiple factors. It is unethical to infect humans experimentally. The postulates also do not apply to noninfectious or chronic diseases.

Modern alternatives include molecular Koch's postulates and the Bradford Hill criteria.

prompt: Identify two strengths and two weaknesses of a case-control study.
answer: Strengths: quick and inexpensive; good for rare diseases and long latency; can study multiple exposures. Weaknesses: recall bias; selection bias in choosing controls; cannot calculate incidence/RR (only OR); temporality can be unclear.
answer_text: Strengths: quick and inexpensive; good for rare diseases and long latency; can study multiple exposures. Weaknesses: recall bias; selection bias in choosing controls; cannot calculate incidence/RR (only OR); temporality can be unclear.
explanation:
Strengths of a case-control study: it is quick and inexpensive; it is efficient for rare diseases and long latency periods; it can study multiple exposures at once; and it needs fewer participants.

Weaknesses: recall bias; selection bias when choosing controls; it cannot calculate incidence or relative risk directly, only the odds ratio; temporality can be unclear; and it is inefficient for rare exposures.

Any two of each answer the question.

prompt: Identify two strengths and two weaknesses of a cross-sectional study.
answer: Strengths: quick and cheap; measures prevalence; can examine many exposures and outcomes; useful for planning and hypothesis generation. Weaknesses: cannot establish temporality (cause vs effect); not good for rare or short-duration diseases; prevalence-incidence (survivor) bias.
answer_text: Strengths: quick and cheap; measures prevalence; can examine many exposures and outcomes; useful for planning and hypothesis generation. Weaknesses: cannot establish temporality (cause vs effect); not good for rare or short-duration diseases; prevalence-incidence (survivor) bias.
explanation:
Strengths of a cross-sectional study: it is quick and cheap; it measures prevalence; it can examine many exposures and outcomes at once; and it is useful for planning and generating hypotheses.

Weaknesses: it cannot establish temporality (which came first, exposure or disease); it is poor for rare or short-duration diseases; and it is prone to prevalence-incidence (survivor) bias, because long-lasting cases are overrepresented.

Examples include NHANES and many national health surveys.

prompt: Identify two strengths and two weaknesses of a randomized controlled trial.
answer: Strengths: gold standard for causation; randomization controls known and unknown confounders; blinding reduces bias. Weaknesses: expensive and time-consuming; ethical limits (cannot assign harmful exposures); strict eligibility limits generalizability; dropouts/noncompliance.
answer_text: Strengths: gold standard for causation; randomization controls known and unknown confounders; blinding reduces bias. Weaknesses: expensive and time-consuming; ethical limits (cannot assign harmful exposures); strict eligibility limits generalizability; dropouts/noncompliance.
explanation:
Strengths of a randomized controlled trial: it is the gold standard for causation; randomization balances known and unknown confounders; and blinding reduces bias.

Weaknesses: it is expensive and time-consuming; there are ethical limits, since researchers cannot assign harmful exposures; strict eligibility criteria limit generalizability; and dropouts and noncompliance can bias results.

RCTs are mainly used to test treatments, vaccines, and preventive interventions.

explanation:
The image is not included, so the answer comes from the wording. An "adjacency" heat map of disease spread risk primarily represents distance-based transmission probability: areas closer to infected areas, or adjacent to them, have higher risk.

Population density (A), vaccination rates (C), and mortality severity (D) could be mapped, but they are not what an adjacency-based spread-risk map shows.

Spatial models that use adjacency or distance help predict where outbreaks may spread next and where to direct resources.

explanation:

Pizza has the highest attack rate, followed by sandwiches. Salad has a low rate.

Food-specific attack rates are the first step in identifying a likely vehicle.

prompt: Identify the most likely source using risk ratio (RR).
answer: Pizza. Assuming the 110 people each ate one item (so non-eaters of a food are the other attendees): Pizza RR = 0.60 / (20/60 = 0.333) = 1.8; Salad RR = 0.167 / (45/80 = 0.5625) = 0.30; Sandwich RR = 0.50 / (35/80 = 0.4375) = 1.14. Pizza has the highest attack rate and RR.

prompt: Calculate the secondary attack rate.
explanation:
Secondary attack rate = secondary cases among contacts ÷ total exposed contacts = 10 ÷ 20 = 50%.

The secondary attack rate measures how readily a disease spreads from primary cases to their contacts. Its denominator is the contacts, not the whole population.

A 50% secondary attack rate among roommates shows how easily influenza spreads in close-contact settings like nursing homes.
scenario_text: An outbreak of influenza occurs in a nursing home with 100 residents. Initial case interviews suggest person-to-person transmission. 10 residents develop influenza after exposure to 20 contacts in shared rooms.

prompt: Identify the mode of transmission.
explanation:
The mode of transmission is person-to-person: direct contact and respiratory droplets from residents sharing rooms.

Influenza spreads mainly through droplets and aerosols from coughing, sneezing, and talking. Contaminated surfaces also contribute.

Shared rooms, close contact with staff, and residents' weaker immunity make nursing homes high-risk settings.
scenario_text: An outbreak of influenza occurs in a nursing home with 100 residents. Initial case interviews suggest person-to-person transmission. 10 residents develop influenza after exposure to 20 contacts in shared rooms.

prompt: Give two prevention strategies, considering biases in interviews.
answer: E.g., vaccinate residents and staff (and antiviral prophylaxis), cohort/isolate ill residents, hand hygiene and masking. To limit interview bias (recall/interviewer bias in elderly residents), use standardized questionnaires and verify exposures with medical/room records.
answer_text: E.g., vaccinate residents and staff (and antiviral prophylaxis), cohort/isolate ill residents, hand hygiene and masking. To limit interview bias (recall/interviewer bias in elderly residents), use standardized questionnaires and verify exposures with medical/room records.
explanation:
Prevention strategies include vaccinating residents and staff; giving antiviral prophylaxis to exposed residents; isolating or cohorting ill residents; and hand hygiene and masking.

Interviews with elderly residents can suffer from recall bias, because memory may be impaired, and from interviewer bias. Standardized questionnaires, and checking exposures against medical and room-assignment records, reduce these biases.

Nursing home flu outbreaks are reportable in many jurisdictions and trigger antiviral prophylaxis for all residents.

prompt: Calculate incidence and prevalence.
answer: Incidence = 100 new cases / 2,000 = 5% per month (50 per 1,000). Prevalence cannot be computed exactly without knowing existing cases; if these are the only current cases, it is also 100/2,000 = 5%.
answer_text: Incidence = 100 new cases / 2,000 = 5% per month (50 per 1,000). Prevalence cannot be computed exactly without knowing existing cases; if these are the only current cases, it is also 100/2,000 = 5%.
explanation:
Incidence = new cases ÷ population = 100 ÷ 2,000 = 5% per month, or 50 per 1,000.

Prevalence can't be calculated exactly without knowing how many cases already existed. If the 100 new cases are the only current cases, prevalence is also 100/2,000 = 5%.

For an acute disease like dengue, illness is short, so prevalence and incidence over a month are similar.
scenario_text: A dengue outbreak occurs in a low-income area with 2,000 residents. 100 new cases are reported this month. Data shows children under 10 are disproportionately affected.

prompt: Identify high-risk groups.
answer: Children under 10 and residents of the low-income area (poor housing, standing water, limited access to repellents/screens).
answer_text: Children under 10 and residents of the low-income area (poor housing, standing water, limited access to repellents/screens).
explanation:
The high-risk groups are children under 10, who are disproportionately affected, and residents of the low-income area.

Low-income areas often have poor housing, standing water such as containers and tires that serve as Aedes mosquito breeding sites, and limited access to screens, repellents, and health care.

Identifying high-risk groups helps target interventions efficiently.

prompt: Suggest one public health intervention.

answer_text: Vector control: eliminate standing water and breeding sites, larvicide/insecticide spraying; or distribute bed nets/repellents and window screens; or community education.
explanation:
Public health interventions for dengue include vector control (eliminating standing water and breeding sites, larviciding, and insecticide spraying), distributing repellents and window screens, and community education.

There's no specific antiviral treatment for dengue, so prevention focuses on the Aedes mosquito vector.

Community engagement is crucial, because many breeding sites are in household containers.

prompt: Give one primordial prevention measure for diabetes.
answer: E.g., policies that prevent risk factors from arising: sugary-drink taxes, healthy school lunch standards, building parks and sidewalks.
answer_text: E.g., policies that prevent risk factors from arising: sugary-drink taxes, healthy school lunch standards, building parks and sidewalks.
explanation:
Primordial prevention stops risk factors from arising in the first place. For diabetes, examples include taxes on sugary drinks, healthy school lunch standards, and urban planning with parks and sidewalks that promote physical activity.

These measures act on social and environmental conditions for the whole population, before individual risk factors such as obesity develop.

Primordial prevention is the earliest level, before primary prevention.
scenario_text: A city tracks diabetes over 10 years. A recent adult exercise program had very low participation.

prompt: Give one primary prevention measure.
answer: E.g., diet and exercise programs for at-risk (overweight/prediabetic) people to prevent diabetes from developing.
answer_text: E.g., diet and exercise programs for at-risk (overweight/prediabetic) people to prevent diabetes from developing.
explanation:
Primary prevention prevents disease from developing in people who may be at risk. For diabetes, examples include diet and exercise programs for overweight or prediabetic individuals.

The Diabetes Prevention Program showed that lifestyle changes reduced the incidence of type 2 diabetes by about 58%.

Primary prevention reduces incidence.
scenario_text: A city tracks diabetes over 10 years. A recent adult exercise program had very low participation.

prompt: Give one secondary prevention measure.
answer: Screening (blood glucose/HbA1c tests) for early detection and treatment.
answer_text: Screening (blood glucose/HbA1c tests) for early detection and treatment.
explanation:
Secondary prevention detects disease early, before symptoms or complications, so treatment can begin promptly. For diabetes, this means screening with blood glucose or HbA1c tests.

Early detection allows treatment that slows progression and prevents complications.

Secondary prevention is effective for diseases with a long asymptomatic phase, like type 2 diabetes.
scenario_text: A city tracks diabetes over 10 years. A recent adult exercise program had very low participation.

prompt: Give one tertiary prevention measure.
answer: Managing diagnosed diabetes to prevent complications: foot care clinics, eye exams, insulin/medication management.
answer_text: Managing diagnosed diabetes to prevent complications: foot care clinics, eye exams, insulin/medication management.
explanation:
Tertiary prevention manages established disease to prevent complications, disability, and death. For diabetes, examples include foot care clinics, regular eye exams, kidney monitoring, and insulin or medication management.

Diabetes complications include blindness, kidney failure, amputations, and heart disease, and tertiary prevention aims to reduce them.

Rehabilitation and disease management programs are tertiary prevention.
scenario_text: A city tracks diabetes over 10 years. A recent adult exercise program had very low participation.

prompt: Give one quaternary prevention measure.
answer: Avoiding overtreatment: e.g., not over-intensifying medications in frail elderly patients (risk of hypoglycemia), avoiding unnecessary tests.
answer_text: Avoiding overtreatment: e.g., not over-intensifying medications in frail elderly patients (risk of hypoglycemia), avoiding unnecessary tests.
explanation:
Quaternary prevention protects patients from overmedicalization: unnecessary or excessive interventions. For diabetes, an example is avoiding overly aggressive glucose lowering in frail elderly patients, which risks dangerous hypoglycemia.

Avoiding unnecessary tests and procedures is also quaternary prevention.

The concept comes from the medical principle "first, do no harm."
scenario_text: A city tracks diabetes over 10 years. A recent adult exercise program had very low participation.

prompt: Identify one problem with the low-participation exercise program.
answer: It does not reach the people who need it (self-selection: likely only already-healthy, motivated adults join), so impact is small; possible barriers include cost, timing, access or awareness.
answer_text: It does not reach the people who need it (self-selection: likely only already-healthy, motivated adults join), so impact is small; possible barriers include cost, timing, access or awareness.
explanation:
The main problem with the low-participation program is that it doesn't reach the people who need it most. People who join voluntarily are likely to be already healthy and motivated, a form of self-selection, so the program has little effect on the population.

Barriers to participation might include cost, inconvenient timing or location, lack of awareness, transportation, or cultural factors.

Program evaluation should look at reach and participation, not just effectiveness among participants.
scenario_text: A city tracks diabetes over 10 years. A recent adult exercise program had very low participation.

prompt: Suggest a solution for the problem.
answer: Remove barriers: free or low-cost sessions at convenient times and locations, workplace-based programs, incentives, community outreach through trusted messengers.

explanation:
Solutions include removing barriers (free or low-cost sessions at convenient times and locations), workplace-based programs, incentives, and community outreach through trusted messengers such as faith leaders and community health workers.

Tailoring programs to the target population's needs and culture increases participation.

Engaging the community in program design also improves uptake.

explanation:
Stool samples testing positive for Cryptosporidium parvum among the suspects corresponds to "verify the diagnosis." Lab testing confirms the cases have the suspected disease.

Verification makes sure investigators are studying the right illness and not a misdiagnosis or lab error.

Cryptosporidium is a chlorine-resistant parasite that causes waterborne outbreaks, such as the 1993 Milwaukee outbreak.

answer_text: Find cases systematically and record information
explanation:
Requesting clinic records, conducting door-to-door surveys, and contacting labs corresponds to "find cases systematically and record information," the active case finding step.

These efforts identify cases that might otherwise go unreported, and the information is recorded in a line listing.

Thorough case finding gives a complete picture of the outbreak's size and distribution.

explanation:
Conducting a cohort study and finding that tap water drinkers were 8 times as likely to become sick corresponds to "evaluate hypotheses epidemiologically." This is analytic epidemiology that tests a hypothesis.

The RR of 8 strongly supports tap water as the source.

The next steps would include reconsidering or refining hypotheses, environmental studies such as water testing, and control measures.

prompt: Public health officials issued an advisory on unhealthy water: citizens must boil tap water before drinking and must repair their filtration systems and water pipes as soon as possible.
explanation:
Issuing a boil-water advisory and requiring filtration and pipe repairs corresponds to "implement control and prevention measures."

Boiling kills Cryptosporidium, which resists chlorine. Fixing the infrastructure prevents future contamination.

Control measures should be implemented as soon as the source is suspected.

prompt: The local health department was to continue reporting cases and test the quality of water weekly.
explanation:
Continuing to report cases and testing water quality weekly corresponds to "initiate or maintain surveillance."

Ongoing surveillance confirms the control measures are working and detects any recurrence.

The final step is communicating findings, through reports to authorities and the public.

prompt: (Tiebreaker) Who conducted the Broad Street Pump study in 1854?
explanation:
John Snow conducted the Broad Street pump study during the 1854 London cholera outbreak.

He mapped cholera deaths, found they clustered around the Broad Street water pump, and persuaded authorities to remove the pump handle.

Snow is considered a founder of modern epidemiology.

answer_text: Joseph Lister (father of modern antiseptic surgery); Ambroise Paré is also commonly given this title.
explanation:
Joseph Lister is commonly called the father of modern antiseptic surgery. He introduced carbolic acid (phenol) to sterilize instruments and clean wounds in the 1860s, which dramatically reduced surgical infections.

Ambroise Paré, a 16th-century French surgeon, is also commonly given the title "father of modern surgery" for his surgical innovations.

Lister's work built on Pasteur's germ theory, and Listerine is named after him.

answer_text: Timmy kept attending daycare for two days while symptomatic (should have been excluded until recovered); or toys/surfaces were not disinfected regularly (should follow a daily cleaning schedule).
explanation:

Clear exclusion policies and cleaning protocols are standard infection control in childcare settings.

prompt: Which of the following characteristics differentiates prions from viruses?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Can replicate independently in a host

answer_text: C) Composed solely of misfolded proteins
explanation:
Prions are made only of misfolded proteins. They have no nucleic acids (DNA or RNA). Viruses contain nucleic acids.

Prions do not contain nucleic acids (A). Neither prions nor viruses replicate independently (B). Both can cause chronic or slowly progressive disease (D).

Prions cause disease by making normal proteins misfold. Examples include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, kuru, and mad cow disease.

prompt: Which of the following fungal diseases is most likely to affect immunocompromised patients?
explanation:
Histoplasmosis, caused by Histoplasma capsulatum inhaled from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings, can become disseminated and life-threatening in immunocompromised patients such as those with HIV/AIDS.

Tinea corporis (A), athlete's foot (C), and ringworm (D) are superficial dermatophyte skin infections that affect healthy people.

Other opportunistic fungal infections include Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, and invasive aspergillosis.
key_note: The others are superficial dermatophyte infections; histoplasmosis becomes disseminated in the immunocompromised.

prompt: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species, which require both human and mosquito hosts. This type of life cycle is classified as:
explanation:
Malaria's Plasmodium requires both human and mosquito hosts, so this is vector-borne transmission. The Anopheles mosquito carries the parasite between humans.

Direct transmission (A) is person-to-person contact. Zoonotic transmission (C) is from animals; humans are the main reservoir for most malaria species. Nosocomial transmission (D) happens in healthcare settings.

This is biological vector transmission, because the parasite develops inside the mosquito.

prompt: What type of bias occurs when cases detected between screening programs have worse prognosis than those detected by screening programs?
explanation:
Length-time bias occurs because screening tends to detect slow-growing disease, which has a long preclinical phase. Fast-growing, aggressive disease tends to appear between screenings as "interval cases" with a worse prognosis.

As a result, screen-detected cases appear to do better even if screening does not change outcomes.

Lead-time bias (C) is a different problem: survival appears longer only because the diagnosis came earlier. Ascertainment bias (B) and attrition bias (D) are unrelated.
key_note: Screening preferentially detects slow-growing disease; fast-growing 'interval cases' appear between screens.

explanation:
Koch's postulates establish a causal relationship between a specific microorganism and a disease.

They do not identify genetic mutations (A), determine treatments (B), or classify microorganisms (D).

They were developed in the 1880s and remain a classic framework, with known limitations.

prompt: A study examines the relationship between diet and lung cancer. Participants with lung cancer are found to be more likely to recall and report their consumption of certain foods compared to healthy controls. What type of bias is this?
explanation:
Participants with lung cancer recalling and reporting their food consumption differently from healthy controls is recall bias.

Selection bias (A) comes from how participants are chosen. Observer bias (C) comes from the investigator. Attrition bias (D) comes from dropouts.

Recall bias is a type of information bias common in case-control studies.

prompt: A local health department receives reports of a Salmonella outbreak from three different restaurants. PFGE is performed on isolates from each location, and the resulting band patterns are identical. What does this indicate?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The isolates likely share a common source or are highly related.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bacteria have identical SNP mutations.

answer_text: B) The isolates likely share a common source or are highly related.
explanation:
Identical PFGE band patterns from isolates at three restaurants mean the isolates are highly related and likely share a common source, such as a shared supplier or ingredient.

They are not unrelated (A). PFGE can assess relatedness (C). PFGE does not detect SNPs (D).

PulseNet used this kind of matching to link geographically separate cases into a single outbreak.

Identical PFGE patterns with slightly different SNP profiles show that PFGE is less sensitive to small genetic differences than SNP analysis.

PFGE detects only large-scale changes that alter restriction fragment sizes. SNP analysis detects single-base differences.

Small SNP differences do not mean the isolates are unrelated (B), from different species (C), or impossible to compare (D).

explanation:
PFGE and SNP mapping work together. PFGE identifies strains with identical banding patterns, and SNP mapping then detects minor genetic differences to work out relationships and the most recent common ancestor.

PFGE screens for matching clusters, and SNP analysis refines who is related to whom.

prompt: A community implements a new policy requiring all restaurants to display calorie counts and provide nutrition education to patrons. This intervention is an example of:
explanation:
The key's answer is primary prevention. A policy requiring calorie labels and nutrition education helps people make healthier choices before disease develops.

Because it is a population-level policy that changes the environment, it could also be called primordial prevention, but that option is not offered.

It is not secondary (screening), tertiary (managing disease), or quaternary (avoiding overtreatment) prevention.
key_note: As a population-level policy it could also be called primordial, but that option is not offered.

explanation:
The key's answer is secondary prevention. Screening patients and following up on blood pressure supports early detection and treatment.

Hypertension is often symptomless, which is why screening and early treatment matter.
