explanation:
Tuberculosis is a chronic disease. Symptoms develop slowly and last or recur over long periods.

Influenza, by contrast, is acute, with sudden onset and short duration.

TB treatment takes 6 months or more.

Examples include latent TB, herpes viruses such as varicella-zoster (which can reactivate as shingles), and HIV's clinical latency.

Latent infections can reactivate when immunity weakens.

prompt: ______________: A single cause leads to a specific effect (though this is less common in complex diseases).
explanation:
Specificity, as a Bradford Hill criterion, means a single cause leads to a specific effect.

It's considered a weak criterion. Many exposures (like smoking) cause several diseases, and many diseases have several causes.

Note that "specificity" isn't in the given word bank, which seems to be an oversight in the test.

prompt: A mortality rate statistically modified to eliminate the effect of different age distributions in the different populations: ________ Mortality Rate.
explanation:
An age-adjusted mortality rate is statistically modified to remove the effect of different age distributions, so populations can be compared fairly.

It's calculated by direct standardization (applying age-specific rates to a standard population) or indirect standardization.

explanation:
Five first questions for a suspected measles case:

prompt: What are two limitations of Koch's postulates?
answer: Some organisms cannot be grown in pure culture (viruses, prions, M. leprae); there may be no animal model of infection; asymptomatic carriers exist; one pathogen can cause several diseases or a disease can have multiple causes; ethics prevent infecting humans.
answer_text: Some organisms cannot be grown in pure culture (viruses, prions, M. leprae); there may be no animal model of infection; asymptomatic carriers exist; one pathogen can cause several diseases or a disease can have multiple causes; ethics prevent infecting humans.
explanation:
Limitations of Koch's postulates include:

- Some organisms can't be grown in pure culture, such as viruses, prions, and M. leprae. - There may be no animal model for the infection. - Asymptomatic carriers exist. - One pathogen can cause several diseases, and some diseases have multiple causes. - Ethics prevent infecting humans to test causation.

Modern alternatives include molecular Koch's postulates and the Bradford Hill criteria.

prompt: Which of the following is not a blood borne pathogen?
explanation:
Bloodborne pathogens spread through contact with infected blood or certain body fluids: needlesticks, shared needles, transfusions, sexual contact, or from mother to baby. HIV and hepatitis B (and hepatitis C) are the classic bloodborne pathogens covered by workplace bloodborne-pathogen rules.

Hepatitis A is spread by the fecal-oral route, through contaminated food, water, or hands, so it is not bloodborne, and B is the intended answer. Tuberculosis is also not bloodborne: it is airborne, spread in droplet nuclei when an infected person coughs. So the question technically has two correct answers.

The bigger lesson is that "hepatitis" covers several viruses with different routes: A and E are fecal-oral, while B, C, and D are bloodborne. Recalling specific pathogens' routes is outside the official event rules, but invitational tests often include it.
key_note: Hepatitis A spreads fecal-oral. Tuberculosis (airborne) is also not bloodborne, so the item has two defensible answers. Pathogen recall is out of scope per rule 3.a.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the retrospective design where subjects are sampled by disease status and is often used when the investigator is interested in rare diseases?
explanation:
A case-control study selects participants by disease status, people with the disease (cases) and without it (controls), and looks back at their past exposures. Because it starts with people who already have the disease, it is efficient for rare diseases: you don't have to follow thousands of people waiting for a few cases to appear.

An intervention trial (A) assigns an exposure and follows people forward. A retrospective cohort (C) also uses past data, but it selects people by exposure status rather than disease. An ecologic study (D) compares groups or populations rather than individuals.

Case-control studies use the odds ratio as their measure of association. Their main weaknesses are recall bias and choosing appropriate controls.

prompt: Characteristics that serve as a general guide to determine which outbreaks deserve further investigation. Choose all that apply.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Outbreaks associated with institutional settings or with a likely (controllable) environmental source

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clusters of infection potentially caused by a bioterrorism agent

choices.label: D
choices.text: When transmission is believed to come from an animal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Outbreaks which have generated excessive public anxiety

choices.label: F
choices.text: Outbreaks which are either very large or rapidly progressing

answer_text: B) Outbreaks associated with institutional settings or with a likely (controllable) environmental source; C) Clusters of infection potentially caused by a bioterrorism agent; E) Outbreaks which have generated excessive public anxiety; F) Outbreaks which are either very large or rapidly progressing
explanation:
Health departments can't fully investigate every cluster, so they prioritize. CDC and state guidance give investigation higher priority when the outbreak is large or spreading rapidly, occurs in an institution (hospital, school, nursing home) or has a likely controllable source, could involve bioterrorism, or is causing high public anxiety. Other reasons include severe disease, a new or unusual agent, a chance to learn something scientifically, and legal or political pressure. B, C, E, and F match these criteria.

A small outbreak within one family (A) usually doesn't need a full investigation; it can be handled with basic advice and control measures. Transmission from an animal (D) isn't, by itself, a standard criterion for priority, although a new zoonosis might qualify as unusual.

The underlying logic is that investigations are worth the resources when they can stop ongoing spread, protect many people, or meet urgent public or security needs.
key_note: Priority goes to outbreaks that are severe, large or rapidly spreading, in institutions, with a controllable source, possibly bioterrorism-related, or causing high public concern. A single-family cluster usually does not warrant a full investigation.

prompt: Key sources of morbidity data include which of the following? (Mark ALL correct answers)
answer_text: B) Hospital discharge data.; C) Laboratory results.; D) Notifiable disease reports.
explanation:
Morbidity data describe illness in a population. Key sources include hospital discharge data (diagnoses of hospitalized patients), laboratory results (confirmed infections), and notifiable disease reports (cases that providers must report by law). Other sources include disease registries, surveys, and emergency department records.

Environmental monitoring data (A), such as air or water quality, measure hazards or exposures, not illness in people. Vital records (E) record births and deaths, so they are sources of natality and mortality data rather than morbidity data (although death certificates list causes of death).

The distinction between morbidity (illness) and mortality (death) data comes up often on tests. Surveillance systems combine many of these sources.
key_note: Vital records (births and deaths) are mortality/natality data; environmental monitoring measures hazards, not illness.

prompt: In a lab study, it was found that by increasing the exposure of toxic gas, there was higher risk that the subjects fell ill. Which of Hill's criteria is this?
explanation:
The dose-response relationship (biological gradient) is the Bradford Hill criterion stating that more exposure leads to more disease, or a higher risk of disease. Finding that higher doses of the toxic gas produce a higher risk of illness is a dose-response relationship.

Specificity (A) means one exposure leads to one particular disease. Temporality (B) means the exposure comes before the disease. Coherence (D) means the causal interpretation fits existing knowledge of the disease's biology and natural history.

A dose-response relationship is strong evidence for causation because it is hard to explain by confounding alone. Classic examples are pack-years of smoking and lung cancer risk, and years of asbestos exposure and mesothelioma.

prompt: The list of diseases that a physician must report to the local health department is typically compiled by the…
explanation:
In the United States, the legal requirement to report diseases comes from state law and regulations, so each state health department sets its own list of reportable (notifiable) diseases. Physicians and labs typically report to the local health department, which passes reports to the state.

Local health departments (A) receive reports but don't usually set the list. CDC (C) and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE, D) jointly maintain the list of nationally notifiable diseases and standard case definitions, but national reporting to CDC is voluntary. States decide what is legally reportable within their borders.

This is why reportable disease lists differ slightly from state to state, even though most states follow the CSTE/CDC national list closely.
key_note: Reporting is mandated by state law/regulation. CSTE and CDC recommend the national notifiable list, but each state sets its own reportable list.

prompt: Which type of surveillance involves reports from health professionals selected to represent a particular area or group?
explanation:
Sentinel surveillance relies on a selected sample of reporting sites, such as particular clinics, physicians, or hospitals, chosen to represent an area or group. These sites report all cases of certain conditions, often weekly, which lets health officials monitor trends without requiring reports from every provider. The influenza-like illness network (ILINet) is a classic example.

Syndromic surveillance (A) tracks symptoms or pre-diagnostic data such as ED complaints or pharmacy sales. Passive surveillance (B) relies on all providers reporting on their own. Active surveillance (D) has the health department reaching out to providers to find cases.

Sentinel systems are cheaper and often produce higher-quality data than trying to collect everything everywhere. The trade-off is that they may not capture rare events or be fully representative.

prompt: Which disease is not an example of herd immunity?
explanation:
Herd immunity protects unvaccinated people when enough of the population is immune that person-to-person transmission can't continue. It only works for diseases that spread from person to person. Polio, measles, pertussis, and diphtheria all spread between people, so vaccinating most of the population protects the rest.

Tetanus is different: it is caused by Clostridium tetani spores in soil and dust that enter wounds. Because tetanus isn't transmitted from person to person, vaccinating others doesn't protect you. Each person is protected only by their own vaccination. Tetanus is therefore the disease that is not an example of herd immunity.

This makes tetanus a useful test case. Herd immunity requires a human-to-human (or human-dependent) chain of transmission that vaccination can interrupt.
key_note: Tetanus is acquired from spores in the environment, not from people, so vaccinating others gives no indirect protection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: microbes are present in a diseased animal.

answer_text: B) specific microbes cause specific diseases.
explanation:
Robert Koch's major contribution was showing that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases. He identified the bacteria causing anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882), and cholera (1883), and formulated Koch's postulates as criteria for linking a particular microbe to a particular disease. This established germ theory on solid experimental footing.

His work did not show that all microbes can be cultured (A); in fact, many can't, which is a limitation of his postulates. Transmission between animals (C) wasn't his key insight. Simply finding microbes in a diseased animal (D) isn't enough, because microbes are everywhere; the point is a specific, consistent causal link.

Koch shares credit for germ theory with Louis Pasteur. Koch also developed key laboratory techniques, including solid culture media (agar plates) and staining methods.

prompt: Symptoms of disease differ from signs of disease in that symptoms:

choices.label: A
choices.text: always occur as part of a syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: are specific for a particular disease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: are changes felt by the patient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: are measurable changes observed by the physician.

answer_text: C) are changes felt by the patient.
explanation:
Symptoms are subjective changes that the patient feels and reports, such as pain, fatigue, nausea, or dizziness. Signs are objective, measurable findings that a clinician can observe or test, such as fever, rash, blood pressure, or abnormal lab results.

Symptoms don't always occur as part of a syndrome (A), and they are often non-specific, shared by many diseases (B). Choice D describes signs, not symptoms.

Clinical criteria in case definitions often combine both, for example "fever ≥ 100.4 °F (sign) and cough (symptom)." Syndromic surveillance tracks patterns of signs and symptoms before diagnoses are confirmed.

prompt: Epidemiological measures include: (Mark ALL correct answers)
answer_text: A) Counts; B) Proportion; C) Ratio; D) Risk; E) Prevalence
explanation:
Epidemiologists measure disease frequency and occurrence with several tools. Counts are the raw number of cases. Ratios compare two quantities (such as male to female cases). Proportions are a part divided by the whole. Risk is the probability of developing disease over a period (incidence proportion). Prevalence is the proportion of a population with the disease at a given time. All five choices are epidemiologic measures.

CDC's Principles of Epidemiology describes counts, ratios, proportions, and rates as the basic measures, with measures like risk, incidence, and prevalence built on them. A proportion is a ratio where the numerator is part of the denominator, and a rate adds a time dimension.

Knowing which measure fits which situation is a core skill. Counts help with planning, rates allow fair comparisons between populations, and ratios like RR compare groups.

prompt: What are the 4 levels of prevention? (Mark ALL correct answers)
answer_text: A) Primordial; B) Primary; C) Secondary; D) Tertiary
explanation:
The classic four levels of prevention are primordial (preventing risk factors from developing), primary (preventing disease in healthy people), secondary (early detection and treatment), and tertiary (reducing complications and disability in established disease).

Quaternary prevention (protecting patients from unnecessary or harmful medical intervention) is also widely recognized. Since the question asks for four levels, quaternary is the one usually left out, but an answer that includes all five is defensible.

Matching examples to levels is common on tests. A smoke-free school policy is primordial, a vaccine is primary, a screening test is secondary, rehabilitation is tertiary, and avoiding an unnecessary scan is quaternary.
key_note: Primordial, primary, secondary and tertiary are the usual four. Quaternary prevention is also recognized, so a five-level answer is defensible.

prompt: An ___________ individual is one whose resistance to infection is impaired by disease, therapy, or burns.
explanation:
An immunocompromised person has a weakened immune system that can't fight infection normally. Causes include diseases (HIV/AIDS, leukemia), treatments (chemotherapy, steroids, transplant medications), severe burns (which destroy the skin barrier and disrupt immunity), malnutrition, and old age.

"Ill" (A) is too general. "Overtreated" (B) refers to excessive medical care. "Hypersensitive" (D) describes an overactive immune response (allergy), the opposite of impaired resistance.

Immunocompromised people are especially susceptible hosts: infections are more severe for them and they can catch opportunistic infections that rarely affect healthy people. They often can't receive live vaccines, so they depend heavily on herd immunity.

prompt: Craig got a deep paper cut and his finger-tip became inflamed. He did not treat the cut and now, 2 weeks later, his whole body hurts. He is tired and pale. What type of infection is this?
explanation:
A systemic infection has spread beyond its original site to affect the whole body, often through the bloodstream. Craig's infection started as local inflammation at the cut, but two weeks later he has whole-body pain, fatigue, and pallor. That means it is now systemic, potentially developing into sepsis.

A local infection (A) stays confined to one area, as the cut did initially. A focal infection (C) is a localized infection that may spread or seed infections elsewhere, but the current picture is body-wide. "Accidental" (D) isn't a type of infection, although the wound itself was an accident.

Clinical classification of infections isn't central to the event rules, but this scenario shows how an untreated local infection can progress. Skin is a major barrier, and breaks in it are portals of entry.

prompt: Epidemiology is concerned with the __________ and __________ of health events in a population:
explanation:
CDC's Lesson 1 states that "epidemiology is concerned with the frequency and pattern of health events in a population." Frequency is how often health events occur (counts and rates), and pattern is their occurrence by person, place, and time. Together these make up the distribution of disease.

The other pairs mix in determinants (the causes and factors that influence occurrence), which are the second half of the formal definition: "the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states." Determinants are about why, while frequency and pattern describe what, who, where, and when.

The full CDC definition: "the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems."
key_note: CDC Lesson 1: 'Epidemiology is concerned with the frequency and pattern of health events in a population.'

prompt: What term describes "illness within a population"?
explanation:
Morbidity means illness or disease in a population: the state of being diseased, or the incidence or prevalence of disease. Morbidity data come from sources like notifiable disease reports, hospital discharge records, and surveys.

Mortality (A) refers to death. A carcinogen (B) is a substance that causes cancer. Virulent (C) describes an agent that causes severe disease.

Morbidity and mortality often appear together, as in CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), which publishes surveillance data and outbreak reports.

prompt: Rabies is an example of a zoonotic disease.
explanation:
A zoonosis is an infectious disease transmitted from animals to humans. Rabies, caused by a lyssavirus, is transmitted mainly through bites from infected animals such as dogs, bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes. It is a classic zoonosis, so the statement is true.

Other well-known zoonoses include Lyme disease (from deer and mice, via ticks), avian influenza, plague (rodents and fleas), salmonellosis from poultry or reptiles, and Ebola (likely bats).

Rabies is almost 100% fatal once symptoms appear, but it is preventable with post-exposure prophylaxis (wound care, rabies immune globulin, and a series of vaccine doses). Controlling rabies in animals, through vaccinating dogs and wildlife bait vaccines, is the main public health strategy.

prompt: For rare diseases (e.g., measles, anthrax), a single case may be considered an outbreak.
explanation:
An outbreak is defined as more cases than expected. For diseases that are normally absent or extremely rare in an area, such as measles in the U.S., anthrax, botulism, or smallpox, even one case exceeds the expected number of zero and may trigger an outbreak investigation. The statement is true.

A single case of a disease like botulism can also signal that others were exposed to the same source, such as a contaminated food. A single smallpox or inhalation anthrax case would be treated as a potential bioterrorism event.

This is why surveillance systems require immediate reporting of certain "single case = emergency" diseases rather than waiting for a cluster.

prompt: In current thinking, the term "epidemic" is used only to describe outbreaks of infectious disease.
explanation:
Originally, "epidemic" referred to outbreaks of infectious disease, but modern epidemiology uses it for any health-related event occurring clearly in excess of normal expectation. That includes noninfectious conditions like the opioid overdose epidemic, the obesity epidemic, or injury and violence epidemics. The statement is false.

CDC defines an epidemic as "the occurrence of more cases of disease than expected in a given area or among a specific group of people over a particular period of time." Nothing in that definition limits it to infections.

Epidemiology itself covers "disease, injury, health, and disability," as the event description says, so its terms apply across infectious and chronic conditions.
key_note: Epidemic now covers any health event above expected levels, e.g. the obesity or opioid epidemics.

prompt: Unfavorable lifestyle patterns can be a determinant for disease development.
explanation:
Determinants are factors that influence the occurrence of disease, including biological, behavioral, social, and environmental factors. Unfavorable lifestyle patterns such as smoking, poor diet, physical inactivity, and heavy alcohol use are well-established determinants of heart disease, diabetes, cancer, and many other conditions. The statement is true.

Lifestyle determinants are a major focus of chronic disease epidemiology and of prevention programs at the primordial and primary levels.

Determinants answer the "why" and "how" of disease, the analytic half of epidemiology, while distribution answers "who, where, and when."

prompt: Epidemiologists always know or find out the determinants for a disease they are researching.
explanation:
Epidemiologists don't always identify the determinants of a disease. Some outbreaks are never solved, and some diseases have causes that remain unknown or only partly understood after decades of research. Many cancers and autoimmune diseases are examples. Studies may be limited by small sample sizes, bias, confounding, or a lack of data. The statement is false.

Even without identifying a cause, epidemiologists can still describe a disease by person, place, and time, find high-risk groups, and recommend control measures. John Snow stopped a cholera outbreak decades before the cholera bacterium was identified.

This is also why causal conclusions require careful judgment (Bradford Hill criteria) and why findings are revised as new evidence appears.

prompt: Epidemiology investigates health phenomena with populations that are diseased only.
explanation:
Epidemiology studies whole populations, both sick and healthy people. Comparing people with and without disease, or with and without an exposure, is how epidemiologists find risk factors. Control groups in case-control studies and unexposed groups in cohort studies are usually healthy. The statement is false.

Epidemiology also studies positive health states and behaviors (such as physical activity or vaccination coverage), not just disease.

The definition refers to "health-related states or events in specified populations," which covers health as well as illness.

prompt: Epidemiology investigates health phenomena that involve not only diseases but also injuries within populations.
explanation:
Epidemiology studies all kinds of health-related states and events, including injuries (car crashes, falls, violence, drowning), disabilities, and other outcomes, not just diseases. The event rules describe the scope as "the scientific study of disease, injury, health, and disability." The statement is true.

Injury epidemiology uses the same methods as infectious disease epidemiology: surveillance, rates, risk factors, and prevention. For example, studies showing that seatbelts and helmets reduce injury and death led to laws that save many lives.

Even the agent-host-environment triad applies to injuries. In a car crash, the agent is kinetic energy, the host is the person, and the environment is the road and vehicle.

prompt: The study base for a case-control study consists of those people who if they developed the disease could have been counted as cases.
explanation:
The study base (source population) of a case-control study is the population from which the cases arise. Ideally, it includes everyone who, if they had developed the disease, would have been identified and counted as a case. Controls should be sampled from this same study base so that they represent the exposure distribution of the population that produced the cases. The statement is true.

If controls come from a different population than the cases, for example cases from the whole city but controls only from one hospital, selection bias can distort the odds ratio.

The general principle for control selection is that controls should be comparable to cases in every way except for having the disease.

prompt: The _______ criteria are the following guidelines: Strength, Consistency, Specificity, Temporality, Biological Gradient, Plausibility, Coherence, Experiment, Analogy. These guidelines are used in epidemiology to assess if an observed association between an exposure and a health outcome is likely causal.
explanation:
The Bradford Hill criteria, proposed by Sir Austin Bradford Hill in 1965, are nine viewpoints for judging whether an observed association is likely causal: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient (dose-response), plausibility, coherence, experiment, and analogy.

They are guidelines, not strict rules. Only temporality is considered essential. Hill developed them while helping establish that smoking causes lung cancer, based on the accumulating epidemiologic evidence.

The event rules ask you to apply these criteria to outbreaks and compare them with Koch's postulates, Evans' postulates, DAGs, sufficient-component cause models, and GRADE. Memorize all nine with an example of each.

prompt: __________________ vaccines are deliberately weakened cell cultures that closely mimic an actual infection and tend to provide better immunity.
explanation:
Live attenuated vaccines contain a weakened form of the living pathogen that can still replicate but doesn't cause serious disease. Because they mimic natural infection closely, they usually produce strong, long-lasting immunity, often after one or two doses. Examples include MMR, varicella (chickenpox), oral polio, and the nasal flu vaccine.

The original question also says "booster shots are examples," which is inaccurate. Boosters are additional doses of any vaccine type given to restore waning immunity; they are not a vaccine category. Inactivated (killed) vaccines, by contrast, usually need multiple doses and boosters.

Live vaccines generally shouldn't be given to immunocompromised people or pregnant women, because even a weakened pathogen could cause disease.
key_note: The original stem also says 'booster shots are examples', which is inaccurate.

prompt: A toxic inflammatory condition arising from the spread of microbes, especially bacteria or their toxins, is termed ___________.
explanation:
Sepsis is a life-threatening, body-wide response to infection. The immune system's reaction to microbes or their toxins in the bloodstream damages the body's own tissues and organs. Untreated, it can progress to septic shock (dangerously low blood pressure) and death.

Sepsis can start from any infection, including pneumonia, urinary tract infections, skin infections (like Craig's cut in Q15), and abdominal infections. Early recognition and treatment with antibiotics and fluids saves lives.

This is a clinical term from the word bank. In epidemiology, sepsis is an important cause of death in hospitals and is often linked to healthcare-associated (nosocomial) infections.

prompt: Chemicals that preserve and increase the efficacy of vaccines and other medical treatments are termed _________________.
explanation:
Adjuvants are substances added to some vaccines to strengthen the immune response, so less antigen or fewer doses are needed. Aluminum salts are the most common adjuvant. The question's wording ("preserve and increase the efficacy") blends adjuvants with preservatives; strictly, preservatives (like thimerosal in multi-dose vials) prevent contamination, while adjuvants boost the immune response.

Adjuvants are especially important in inactivated and subunit vaccines (hepatitis B, HPV, DTaP), which on their own provoke weaker responses than live vaccines.

Vaccine composition is outside the core event rules but appears on invitational tests as vocabulary.

prompt: Typhoid Mary is considered a(n) ________________ carrier.
explanation:
Mary Mallon ("Typhoid Mary") was an Irish-born cook in New York in the early 1900s who carried Salmonella Typhi in her body for years without symptoms. She infected dozens of people through the food she prepared. She was an asymptomatic (healthy) carrier and, because she shed bacteria for years, a chronic carrier.

Carriers are a crucial link in the chain of infection because they don't know they are infectious and keep exposing others. Mallon refused to stop working as a cook and was eventually quarantined for most of her life.

Her case raised lasting public health questions about balancing individual liberty with protecting the community, and it is why food handlers can be excluded from work when they carry certain pathogens.

prompt: A process that begins when an agent leaves its reservoir or host through a portal of exit, and is conveyed by some mode of transmission, then enters through an appropriate portal of entry to infect a susceptible host: ___________ of ______________
explanation:
The chain of infection describes how an infectious agent spreads: it leaves its reservoir through a portal of exit, travels by a mode of transmission, enters a susceptible host through a portal of entry, and causes infection. The six links are agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. CDC also calls this the chain of transmission.

Interrupting any link breaks the chain. Control measures map to specific links: treating the reservoir, blocking portals (masks, condoms), interrupting transmission (handwashing, water treatment, vector control), and protecting hosts (vaccination).

The event rules list "the agent, host, environment triad and chain of transmission." Expect to apply the chain to a specific disease in a case study.

prompt: A well-defined group of people who have had a common experience or exposure, who are then followed up for the incidence of new diseases or events, as in a cohort or prospective study: _________
explanation:
A cohort is a well-defined group of people who share a common experience or exposure (born in the same year, worked in the same factory, attended the same event) and are followed over time to measure the incidence of new disease. Cohort studies compare outcomes between exposed and unexposed members.

The word comes from Roman military units. In epidemiology, a cohort can be closed (fixed membership, like attendees of a banquet) or open (people enter and leave, like residents of a city).

Famous cohort studies include the Framingham Heart Study (1948 onward) and the British Doctors Study on smoking.

prompt: A range of values for a variable of interest, e.g., a rate, constructed so that this range has a specified probability of including the true value of the variable. The specified probability is called the __________ level.
explanation:
A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values, calculated from the study data, that is likely to contain the true value of a measure such as a rate, RR, or OR. The confidence level (usually 95%) is the specified probability that intervals constructed this way would include the true value if the study were repeated many times.

Confidence intervals show both precision and statistical significance. A narrow CI means a precise estimate. For RR or OR, a 95% CI that includes 1.0 means the result isn't statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

For example, RR = 3.2 with a 95% CI of 1.1 to 9.6 is significant (it excludes 1) but imprecise (wide). Larger studies give narrower intervals.

prompt: ____________ infection: rapid onset of symptoms, followed by a brief set of symptoms and a resolution within days.
explanation:
An acute infection has a rapid onset, a relatively short course of symptoms, and resolution within days to weeks. Examples include influenza, strep throat, and most food poisoning.

Chronic infections persist for long periods (hepatitis B, HIV, tuberculosis). Latent infections remain dormant and can reactivate later (herpes simplex, varicella-zoster causing shingles).

Acute infectious diseases dominate outbreak investigations and epi curves, while chronic diseases are studied with longer-term designs such as cohort and case-control studies.

prompt: If 18 people in 18 different households became ill with shigellosis in a community of 1,000 people, the attack rate would be _______% (tenth place).
explanation:
The attack rate is the number of people who became ill divided by the population at risk: 18 ÷ 1,000 = 0.018, or 1.8%.

The detail about 18 different households tells you each case was in a separate household. That means the cases are not explained by household spread and suggests a community-wide source. It doesn't change the calculation.

Attack rates are usually expressed as percentages, and the denominator is the population at risk (here, the whole community). Be careful to round to the place requested; here that is the tenths place.

prompt: Changes over a long period of time, generally years or decades: ___________ trend.
explanation:
A secular trend is a long-term change in the occurrence of a disease or health event over years or decades. Examples are the decline in heart disease deaths since the 1960s and the rise in obesity since the 1980s.

Secular trends are distinct from seasonal variation (yearly cycles, such as influenza peaking in winter) and short-term epidemics (sharp increases over days or weeks).

Interpreting a secular trend requires care. Changes in diagnosis, case definitions, reporting, or population age structure can create apparent trends that aren't real changes in disease occurrence.

prompt: Natural history of a disease classifies into five stages: underlying, _________, subclinical, ________, and recovery/________/death.
explanation:
The natural history of disease runs from a stage of susceptibility (the person is healthy but at risk, with underlying risk factors present), through exposure, to subclinical disease (pathologic changes without symptoms), then clinical disease (symptoms present), and finally an outcome of recovery, disability, or death. The blanks are therefore susceptibility (or exposure), clinical, and disability, all from the word bank.

This sequence matches CDC's natural history diagram, which marks key events between stages: exposure, pathologic changes, onset of symptoms, and the usual time of diagnosis.

Each stage corresponds to a level of prevention: susceptibility to primary prevention, subclinical disease to secondary (screening), and clinical disease to tertiary.

prompt: The natural history of disease consists of five stages of disease: _________, incubation, __________, acute, and _____________.
explanation:
For infectious diseases, the course of illness is often described as incubation (no symptoms), prodromal (early, vague symptoms like fatigue or mild fever), acute or illness phase (full symptoms), decline, and convalescence (recovery). In this question, the first blank comes before incubation, so it is the stage of susceptibility (or exposure). The middle blank is prodromal, and the last is convalescence.

The question's five-stage wording mixes two frameworks: CDC's natural history stages and the clinical stages of infection. Recognizing both helps with ambiguous questions like this one.

The prodromal stage matters epidemiologically because people are often contagious then but don't realize they are getting sick, as with measles before the rash appears.
key_note: The stages of infectious disease are incubation, prodromal, acute (illness), decline and convalescence. The first blank precedes incubation, so it is the susceptible/exposure stage.

prompt: Autism is known as a "___________" disorder because there is wide variation in the type and severity of symptoms people experience.
explanation:
Autism is called a spectrum disorder (autism spectrum disorder, ASD) because people vary widely in the type and severity of their symptoms and in the support they need. The same word, spectrum, is used in epidemiology for the "spectrum of disease," the range of manifestations from inapparent to severe for any condition.

Autism is not part of the event's core content, but the idea of a disease spectrum is. Many infections range from asymptomatic to fatal, and surveillance that only counts severe cases sees only "the tip of the iceberg."

As the question notes, ASD occurs in all genders, racial and ethnic groups, and income levels.

prompt: He designed the first human experiment with controls while studying the treatment of scurvy by eating citrus fruit in 1747. (last name only)
explanation:
James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, conducted one of the first controlled clinical experiments in 1747 aboard HMS Salisbury. He divided 12 sailors with scurvy into six pairs, gave each pair a different treatment, and found that those given oranges and lemons recovered dramatically. (The question says 1740.)

His study had a key feature of modern trials, a comparison between treatment groups, though it lacked randomization and blinding. Decades later the British Navy began issuing citrus juice to sailors, nearly eliminating scurvy.

The first true randomized controlled trial is usually credited to the 1948 Medical Research Council trial of streptomycin for tuberculosis.
key_note: The test says 1740; Lind's scurvy trial was in 1747.

prompt: A. What mode of spread does this epi curve describe? B. This type of epidemic occurs when people are exposed to the same exposure over a ______ period of time. (limited, undetermined, or long)
answer: A. Point source (common source); B. limited (brief)
answer_text: A. Point source (common source); B. limited (brief)
explanation:
This epi curve shows a single, tight peak (cases clustered over about a week) with a couple of outliers before and after. That is the pattern of a point-source (common-source) outbreak, in which a group is exposed to the same source over a limited, brief period, such as a single meal.

A continuous common-source outbreak would show a plateau from a long exposure. A propagated outbreak would show multiple waves.

Outliers are worth investigating. An early case might be the source, such as an infected food handler. A late case might be a secondary person-to-person case or someone with a longer incubation period.
key_note: One tight peak (days ~17-26) with an early and a late outlier is the classic point-source curve.
scenario_text: Epi curve for question 41.

prompt: First person to explain disease occurrence from a rational rather than a supernatural viewpoint. (last name only)
explanation:
Hippocrates (about 460-370 BCE) was the first person known to argue that disease has natural, rational causes rather than supernatural ones. In "On Airs, Waters, and Places," he described how environment, climate, water, and lifestyle relate to disease, and he distinguished endemic from epidemic disease.

This is why Hippocrates is sometimes called the first epidemiologist. He emphasized careful observation of patients and their surroundings, a forerunner of the person-place-time approach.

Other key figures in the history of epidemiology include John Graunt (vital statistics), James Lind (controlled experiment), William Farr (surveillance), John Snow (field epidemiology), and Koch and Pasteur (germ theory).

prompt: Attack rate is also known as _________ proportion.
explanation:
The attack rate is an incidence proportion (cumulative incidence): the number of new cases during a specified period divided by the population at risk at the start of that period. In outbreak settings the period is short, so it's called an "attack rate."

Strictly speaking, it's a proportion, not a true rate, because it has no person-time denominator. The incidence rate (incidence density) divides by person-time.

The secondary attack rate is a related measure: the proportion of contacts of a primary case who develop disease.

prompt: A/an _____ disease is present at a continuous level throughout a population/geographic area.
explanation:
An endemic disease is constantly present at its usual level within a population or geographic area, for example malaria in many tropical regions or chickenpox before the vaccine era.

Endemic doesn't mean low. Endemic levels can be hypoendemic (low), hyperendemic (persistently high), or holoendemic (nearly everyone infected early in life). An epidemic is an increase above the endemic baseline.

Knowing the endemic baseline is essential for deciding whether an outbreak is happening, which is the second step of an outbreak investigation ("establish the existence of an outbreak").

prompt: A disease is _____ when no signs or symptoms are shown. The patient can still be a carrier of the disease.
explanation:
An asymptomatic infection shows no signs or symptoms, but the infected person can still harbor and transmit the agent, making them a carrier. Typhoid Mary is the classic example. Asymptomatic transmission was also a major feature of COVID-19.

Asymptomatic cases are part of the "iceberg" of disease. Surveillance based on symptoms or diagnoses misses them, so true infection rates are usually higher than reported cases.

Identifying asymptomatic carriers, through testing contacts or screening food handlers or healthcare workers, can be crucial for stopping an outbreak.

prompt: ___________ is the proportion of persons with clinical disease who become severely ill or die.
explanation:
Virulence is the proportion of people with clinical disease who become severely ill or die. It measures how severe the disease is among those who are sick.

Don't confuse it with infectivity (the proportion of exposed people who become infected) or pathogenicity (the proportion of infected people who develop clinical disease). The case-fatality rate is related, as the proportion of cases who die, and is a common way to measure the most extreme form of virulence.

Example: rabies has extremely high virulence (nearly all clinical cases die). The common cold has very low virulence.

prompt: ________ is the study of the distribution and determinants of health related states or events in specific populations and the application of this study to the control of health problems.
explanation:
Epidemiology is "the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems" (CDC, after Last's Dictionary of Epidemiology).

Each part matters. Distribution is who, where, and when (descriptive epidemiology). Determinants are the causes and risk factors (analytic epidemiology). Health-related states include disease, injury, disability, and health behaviors. Populations, not individuals, are the focus. Application means epidemiology is meant to guide action.

This definition is foundational, and many test questions ask about one of its pieces.

prompt: The most effective barrier to infection is intact _______.
explanation:
Intact skin is the body's most important physical barrier against infection. Its tough outer layer, acidic surface, normal flora, and constant shedding keep most microbes out. Breaks in the skin (cuts, burns, insect bites, needles, surgical incisions) create portals of entry.

That's why burns and surgical wounds carry high infection risk, why tetanus enters through wounds (Q8 in other tests), and why bloodborne pathogens need a break in the skin or mucous membranes to infect.

Mucous membranes (eyes, nose, mouth, genital tract) are thinner, more vulnerable barriers and are common portals of entry for many pathogens.

prompt: Vital statistics provide an archive of certain health data. These data do not become surveillance data until they are analyzed, interpreted, and disseminated with the intent of influencing _______ _______ decision-making or action.
explanation:
CDC notes that vital statistics (birth and death records) are an archive of health data. They only become surveillance data when they are analyzed, interpreted, and disseminated with the intent of influencing public health decision-making or action.

This reflects the core idea of surveillance: data collection alone isn't surveillance. Surveillance is "information for action," and the five steps end with dissemination and linking the data to public health action.

The same logic applies to all data sources. Hospital records or lab results become surveillance data when they are used systematically to monitor health and guide public health responses.

prompt: A _____ is a spore-producing eukaryote. It lacks chlorophyll; examples include molds, yeasts, mildews, smuts, and mushrooms.
explanation:
Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that lack chlorophyll and reproduce by spores. They include molds, yeasts, mildews, smuts, and mushrooms. Disease-causing fungi include Candida (thrush and yeast infections), dermatophytes (ringworm, athlete's foot), Histoplasma, Aspergillus, and Pneumocystis.

Fungal infections are especially dangerous for immunocompromised people, and some fungi such as Candida auris have caused outbreaks in healthcare settings.

The event rules list fungal diseases among the infectious causes (bacterial, viral, fungal, protist, and prion) to understand in broad terms.

prompt: The _____ case is the first patient in an epidemiological study (also known as patient zero or primary case).
explanation:
The index case is the first case of a disease to come to the attention of investigators, often called "patient zero." Strictly speaking, the primary case is the person who first brought the disease into the population, and investigators sometimes find that the primary case occurred before the index case.

Secondary cases are those infected by the primary case. Tracing back from the index case helps identify the source and route of an outbreak.

Tests often ask about the index/primary distinction, so learn both terms. The question's wording treats them as synonyms, which is common in less formal usage.

prompt: ______ is an illness that is caused by a medication or physician. ______ infections are acquired during the process of receiving health care and were not present at the time of admission.
explanation:
Iatrogenic illness is caused by medical treatment or by a healthcare provider, for example side effects of medications, surgical complications, or infections from procedures. Nosocomial (healthcare-associated) infections are acquired while receiving healthcare and were not present or incubating on admission, such as central-line bloodstream infections or MRSA wound infections.

The two overlap: a nosocomial infection caused by a procedure is also iatrogenic. Iatrogenic is broader (it includes non-infectious harms), while nosocomial refers specifically to infections acquired in healthcare settings.

Hospital infection control programs use surveillance, hand hygiene, sterile technique, and antibiotic stewardship to reduce these infections.

prompt: Herd immunity _________ is the percentage of people who need to be immune in order to achieve herd immunity; it varies with each disease.
explanation:
The herd immunity threshold (HIT) is the proportion of a population that must be immune to stop sustained transmission. It depends on how contagious the disease is: HIT = 1 − 1/R0. Measles (R0 about 15) needs about 93%, polio (R0 about 5 to 7) about 80 to 85%, and seasonal flu (R0 about 1.3) much less.

Because vaccines aren't 100% effective, the vaccination coverage needed is HIT divided by vaccine effectiveness, which is higher than the HIT itself.

When immunity falls below the threshold, especially in clustered pockets of unvaccinated people, outbreaks can occur even if national coverage looks high.

prompt: MDPH recruiting hospitals to report influenza-like illnesses every week is an example of ______ surveillance.
explanation:
Sentinel surveillance uses selected reporting sites, here hospitals recruited by the Massachusetts Department of Public Health (MDPH), that report all cases of a condition (influenza-like illness) on a regular schedule. Tracking trends at these sites gives a picture of flu activity across the state without requiring every provider to report.

It isn't passive surveillance, because the sites are recruited and report on schedule. It isn't syndromic surveillance in the automated sense, although ILI is a syndrome. It differs from active surveillance in that the health department isn't contacting all providers to find cases.

CDC's national ILINet is a sentinel system of outpatient providers who report weekly the number of patients seen with influenza-like illness.

prompt: For the following prevention strategies, indicate which of the levels of prevention (primordial, primary, secondary, or tertiary) they are examples of. A. Screening for high blood pressure; B. Targeted smoking cessation programs; C. Rehabilitation of stroke patients.
answer: A. Secondary; B. Primary; C. Tertiary
answer_text: A. Secondary; B. Primary; C. Tertiary
explanation:
Screening for high blood pressure detects hypertension early, often before symptoms, so it is secondary prevention. Targeted smoking cessation programs help smokers quit before smoking-related disease develops, so they are primary prevention (they remove a risk factor in people who don't yet have the disease). Rehabilitation of stroke patients reduces disability in people who already had a stroke, so it is tertiary prevention.

Ask whether the person has the disease yet and whether they know it: no disease means primary (or primordial for population-level risk-factor prevention), unrecognized disease means secondary, and diagnosed disease means tertiary.

Smoking cessation is sometimes argued to be secondary if the person already has early lung damage, but on standard tests it is primary.

prompt: Match each label on the timeline to: onset of symptoms, point of exposure, screening. A.______ B.______ C.______
answer: A. Point of exposure; B. Onset of symptoms; C. Screening
answer_text: A. Point of exposure; B. Onset of symptoms; C. Screening
explanation:
On CDC's natural history timeline, exposure marks the transition from susceptibility to subclinical disease (arrow A). Screening (arrow C) is aimed at the "detectable subclinical disease" window, when pathologic changes are present but symptoms haven't appeared. Onset of symptoms (arrow B) marks the start of clinical disease, after which diagnosis is usually sought.

This diagram connects prevention to natural history. Primary prevention acts before exposure, secondary prevention (screening) during the detectable subclinical period, and tertiary prevention during clinical disease.

A screening test is only useful if a detectable preclinical phase exists and treating disease early improves outcomes.

prompt: ____ is the habitat in which an infectious agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies, which can include humans, animals, or the environment.
explanation:
The reservoir is the habitat in which an infectious agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies. Reservoirs can be human (measles, smallpox), animal (rabies, plague), or environmental (soil for tetanus, water for Legionella).

The reservoir is not necessarily the source of a particular infection. For example, the reservoir of Salmonella may be chickens, while the source of an outbreak might be contaminated potato salad. The reservoir is where the agent persists naturally.

Diseases with only a human reservoir and no long-term carriers (smallpox, polio) are candidates for eradication. Diseases with animal or environmental reservoirs can't be eradicated by vaccinating people alone.

prompt:
Agents may be biological, chemical or physical. Type "B" for Biological, "C" for Chemical, and "P" for Physical agents.

| Disease | Agent | Type |
|---|---|---|
| First degree burns | Fire | ____ |
| Acute Liver Disease | Hepatitis A | ____ |
| Blindness | Optical Radiation | ____ |
answer: Fire: P; Hepatitis A: B; Optical radiation: P
answer_text: Fire: P; Hepatitis A: B; Optical radiation: P
explanation:
Agents of disease can be biological (living organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites), chemical (toxins, drugs, pollutants, alcohol), or physical (heat, radiation, mechanical force, noise).

Fire causing burns is a physical agent (heat energy). Hepatitis A virus causing liver disease is a biological agent. Optical radiation causing blindness is a physical agent (radiation energy).

This classification extends the agent-host-environment triad to noninfectious diseases and injuries. Chemical agents include lead and carbon monoxide; physical agents include UV light, noise, and the kinetic energy in crashes.

prompt: In an outbreak of gastroenteritis among attendees of a corporate picnic, 99 persons ate potato salad, 30 of whom developed gastroenteritis. Calculate the attack rate of illness among persons who ate potato salad. _________% (tenth place)
explanation:
The attack rate among people who ate potato salad = ill eaters ÷ all eaters = 30 ÷ 99 = 0.303, or 30.3%.

To judge whether potato salad caused the outbreak, compare this with the attack rate among people who didn't eat it and calculate a relative risk. A high attack rate among eaters with a low rate among non-eaters would implicate the potato salad.

This example comes from CDC training materials on food-specific attack rates. Round to the place requested (tenths here).

prompt: 153 people are tested for mononucleosis. There are 36 positive results. Of these 36 positive results, there are 25 true positive results. Of the 117 negative results, there are 109 true negatives. Calculate as percentages rounded to one decimal place: a) Positive Predictive Value; b) Negative Predictive Value.
explanation:
Positive predictive value (PPV) is the proportion of positive test results that are true positives: 25 ÷ 36 = 0.694, or 69.4%. Negative predictive value (NPV) is the proportion of negative results that are true negatives: 109 ÷ 117 = 0.932, or 93.2%.

The test's sensitivity and specificity can also be found. True positives = 25, false positives = 36 − 25 = 11, true negatives = 109, false negatives = 117 − 109 = 8. Sensitivity = 25/33 = 75.8%; specificity = 109/120 = 90.8%.

Predictive values depend on how common the disease is among those tested. As prevalence rises, PPV rises and NPV falls. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test itself.

prompt: CDC and others recognize that the health of people is connected to the health of animals and the environment. There is a movement for partnerships between physicians, veterinarians, and other scientific health disciplines. What is this initiative called?
explanation:
One Health is the collaborative approach, promoted by CDC, WHO, and others, which recognizes that human health is connected to the health of animals and the shared environment. It brings together physicians, veterinarians, ecologists, and public health professionals.

One Health is especially important for zoonotic diseases (about 60% of infectious diseases), antimicrobial resistance, food safety, and emerging infections such as avian influenza, Ebola, and COVID-19.

Examples include monitoring bird flu in poultry and wild birds to protect humans, and coordinating rabies control between animal and human health agencies.

prompt: Malaria cases are reported every year at predictable levels in a specific region of sub-Saharan Africa. The number of cases remains relatively constant from year to year.
explanation:
Malaria cases occurring every year at predictable, relatively constant levels in a specific region describe an endemic disease: one constantly present at its usual level in a population or area.

The key word is "predictable" or "constant." An outbreak or epidemic would mean cases above the usual level, and a pandemic would mean spread across many countries.

Malaria is endemic in much of sub-Saharan Africa, where it is often hyperendemic or holoendemic.

A summer camp that normally sees 1-2 food poisoning cases per season suddenly has 18 campers ill after the same dinner. That's more cases than expected in a specific place, time, and group, which makes it an outbreak.

"Outbreak" is the usual term for a localized increase above expected levels. "Epidemic" covers larger areas and populations.

Distinguishing outbreak, epidemic, and pandemic usually comes down to geographic scale.

prompt: John Snow's investigation of cholera helped establish epidemiology by:
